title: Tell me about yourself

content.overview: Introduce yourself by summarizing your experience, core technical skills, major achievements, and career goals in a concise and confident manner.
content.approach: Start with your experience, highlight your technical expertise, mention measurable achievements, and conclude with why you're looking for your next opportunity.
content.interviewAnswer: Hello, I'm Manikandan Dhanapal. I have 10+ years of experience in software development, including more than 6 years specializing in frontend development using React.js. Throughout my career, I have built scalable, high-performance web applications for e-commerce and enterprise domains, with a strong focus on delivering maintainable and user-friendly solutions. In my recent roles, I have been responsible for designing and developing reusable UI components, implementing state management using Redux Toolkit and Context API, integrating REST APIs and GraphQL, and improving application performance through techniques such as code splitting, lazy loading, memoization, virtualization, and API caching. I also have hands-on experience with modern frontend technologies, including Next.js (SSR, SSG, and ISR), TypeScript, Micro Frontend architecture, React Query, and CI/CD pipelines with cloud-based deployments. I have worked closely with cross-functional teams, participated in code reviews, mentored developers, and collaborated with designers, backend engineers, QA teams, and product owners to deliver high-quality applications. One of my key achievements was improving the application's performance by increasing the Lighthouse score from around 60 to over 90 through bundle optimization, lazy loading, image optimization, and eliminating unnecessary re-renders. Currently, I am looking for an opportunity as a Technical Lead, where I can leverage my technical expertise, mentor team members, contribute to architecture decisions, and help build scalable, high-performance products.
keyPoints: Summarize your experience and technical skills.
Mention your career goals and what you're looking for in your next opportunity.
examples: Focus on experience, achievements, and future goals instead of personal details.

title: Difference Between var, let, and const

content.overview: var is function-scoped, allows re-declaration and re-assignment, and is hoisted with undefined. let is block-scoped, allows re-assignment but not re-declaration, and has a Temporal Dead Zone. const is block-scoped, does not allow re-assignment or re-declaration, must be initialized during declaration, but object and array contents can still be modified.
content.interviewAnswer: var is function-scoped, allows re-declaration and re-assignment, and is hoisted with undefined. let is block-scoped, allows re-assignment but not re-declaration, and has a Temporal Dead Zone. const is block-scoped, does not allow re-assignment or re-declaration, must be initialized during declaration, but object and array contents can still be modified.
keyPoints: var is function-scoped, let and const are block-scoped.
var allows re-declaration and re-assignment, let allows re-assignment but not re-declaration, const allows neither.
var is hoisted with undefined, let and const have a Temporal Dead Zone.
const must be initialized during declaration, but object and array contents can still be modified.
whenToUse: Use var for function-scoped variables (legacy code).
Use let for block-scoped variables that may change.
Use const for block-scoped variables that should not be reassigned.
examples: var: function example() { var x = 1; if (true) { var x = 2; console.log(x); } console.log(x); } // Outputs: 2, 2
let: function example() { let x = 1; if (true) { let x = 2; console.log(x); } console.log(x); } // Outputs: 2, 1
const: const x = 1; x = 2; // Error: Assignment to constant variable.

title: What are Closures?

content.overview: A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has finished execution.
content.interviewAnswer: A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has finished execution.
keyPoints: Closures allow functions to access variables from their outer scope.
They are created every time a function is created.
Closures can lead to memory leaks if not handled properly.
examples: basic: function outer() { let count = 0; return function inner() { count++; return count; }; } const counter = outer(); console.log(counter()); // 1 console.log(counter()); // 2

dataHiding: function createCounter() { let count = 0; return { increment: function() { count++; }, getCount: function() { return count; } }; } const counter = createCounter(); counter.increment(); console.log(counter.getCount()); // 1

title: How Async/Await Works

content.overview: Async/Await is syntactic sugar over Promises. An async function always returns a Promise. await pauses execution until the Promise settles and resumes through the Microtask Queue. It does not block the main thread. Promise.all() should be used for concurrent independent operations.
content.interviewAnswer: Async/Await is syntactic sugar over Promises. An async function always returns a Promise. await pauses execution until the Promise settles and resumes through the Microtask Queue. It does not block the main thread. Promise.all() should be used for concurrent independent operations.

whenToUse: Use async/await for sequential asynchronous operations.
Use Promise.all() for concurrent independent operations.
keyPoints: Await pauses execution until the Promise settles.
Await does not block the main thread.

examples.asyncAwait: async function fetchData() { try { const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data'); const data = await response.json(); console.log(data); } catch (error) { console.error('Error fetching data:', error); } } fetchData();
examples.promiseAll: async function fetchMultipleData() { try { const [data1, data2] = await Promise.all([fetch('https://api.example.com/data1').then(res => res.json()), fetch('https://api.example.com/data2').then(res => res.json())]); console.log(data1, data2); } catch (error) { console.error('Error fetching data:', error); } } fetchMultipleData();
examples.sequential: async function fetchSequentialData() { try { const response1 = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data1'); const data1 = await response1.json(); console.log(data1); const response2 = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data2'); const data2 = await response2.json(); console.log(data2); } catch (error) { console.error('Error fetching data:', error); } } fetchSequentialData();

title: Explain Hoisting

content.overview: Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of processing declarations before execution. var is initialized with undefined. let and const remain in the Temporal Dead Zone. Function declarations are fully hoisted while function expressions are not.
content.interviewAnswer: Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of processing declarations before execution. var is initialized with undefined. let and const remain in the Temporal Dead Zone. Function declarations are fully hoisted while function expressions are not.

title: Are let and const hoisted?

content.overview: Yes, but they remain in the Temporal Dead Zone until initialized.
content.interviewAnswer: Yes, but they remain in the Temporal Dead Zone until initialized.

title: What is the Temporal Dead Zone?

content.overview: The period between scope creation and variable initialization where accessing a let or const variable throws a ReferenceError.
content.interviewAnswer: The period between scope creation and variable initialization where accessing a let or const variable throws a ReferenceError.

title: Why does var return undefined?

content.overview: Because JavaScript initializes var variables with undefined during the memory creation phase.
content.interviewAnswer: Because JavaScript initializes var variables with undefined during the memory creation phase.

title: Why are function declarations callable before declaration?

content.overview: Because the entire function definition is stored in memory during the creation phase.
content.interviewAnswer: Because the entire function definition is stored in memory during the creation phase.

title: Function Declaration vs Function Expression Hoisting

content.overview: Function declarations are fully hoisted. Function expressions behave like variables and only their declaration is hoisted.
content.interviewAnswer: Function declarations are fully hoisted. Function expressions behave like variables and only their declaration is hoisted.

title: What is Callback Hell?

content.overview: Callback Hell occurs when multiple asynchronous operations are nested inside one another using callbacks, making code difficult to read and maintain. Modern JavaScript uses Promises and async/await to solve this problem.
content.interviewAnswer: Callback Hell occurs when multiple asynchronous operations are nested inside one another using callbacks, making code difficult to read and maintain. Modern JavaScript uses Promises and async/await to solve this problem.

title: Promise vs Async/Await

content.overview: Promises represent asynchronous operations using then/catch. Async/await provides cleaner syntax built on top of Promises. Promise APIs such as Promise.all() remain useful for concurrent execution.
content.interviewAnswer: Promises represent asynchronous operations using then/catch. Async/await provides cleaner syntax built on top of Promises. Promise APIs such as Promise.all() remain useful for concurrent execution.

title: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled

content.overview: Promise.all fails fast if any Promise rejects. Promise.allSettled waits for every Promise to complete and returns the status of each.
content.interviewAnswer: Promise.all fails fast if any Promise rejects. Promise.allSettled waits for every Promise to complete and returns the status of each.

title: Debouncing vs Throttling

content.overview: Debouncing delays execution until activity stops. Throttling limits execution to once during a specified interval.
content.interviewAnswer: Debouncing delays execution until activity stops. Throttling limits execution to once during a specified interval.

title: Difference Between call, apply and bind

content.overview: call() invokes immediately with arguments individually. apply() invokes immediately with arguments as an array. bind() returns a new function with this permanently bound.
content.interviewAnswer: call() invokes immediately with arguments individually. apply() invokes immediately with arguments as an array. bind() returns a new function with this permanently bound.

title: What is Shadow DOM?

content.overview: Shadow DOM encapsulates HTML, CSS, and JavaScript inside a component to prevent style and script leakage.
content.interviewAnswer: Shadow DOM encapsulates HTML, CSS, and JavaScript inside a component to prevent style and script leakage.

title: substring vs slice vs substr

content.overview: substring() does not support negative indexes. slice() supports negative indexes and is recommended. substr() uses length and is deprecated.
content.interviewAnswer: substring() does not support negative indexes. slice() supports negative indexes and is recommended. substr() uses length and is deprecated.

title: Is JavaScript Tightly Coupled or Loosely Coupled?

content.overview: JavaScript promotes loose coupling through modular programming, first-class functions, dependency injection, and event-driven architecture.
content.interviewAnswer: JavaScript promotes loose coupling through modular programming, first-class functions, dependency injection, and event-driven architecture.

title: Find Sum Without Loop

content.overview: Find the sum of all elements in an array without using a loop.
content.approach: The two common approaches are using Array.reduce() or recursion.
content.interviewAnswer: Without using loops, the preferred solution is Array.reduce() because it is concise and efficient. Alternatively, recursion can be used to demonstrate an understanding of recursive problem solving.
keyPoints: Do not use for, while, or forEach loops.
Array.reduce() is the most readable solution.
content.spaceComplexity: O(1) using reduce(), O(n) using recursion due to the call stack.

title: Deep Copy vs Shallow Copy

content.overview: A shallow copy copies only the first level. A deep copy recursively copies all nested objects.
content.interviewAnswer: A shallow copy copies only the first level. A deep copy recursively copies all nested objects.

title: JavaScript Event Loop

content.overview: JavaScript uses a Call Stack, Microtask Queue, Macro task Queue, and Event Loop to execute asynchronous code without blocking the main thread.
content.interviewAnswer: JavaScript uses a Call Stack, Microtask Queue, Macro task Queue, and Event Loop to execute asynchronous code without blocking the main thread.

title: Browser Rendering Pipeline

content.overview: The browser rendering pipeline converts HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into visible pixels. The browser first parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM. These are combined to create the Render Tree. Next, Layout (or Reflow) calculates element sizes and positions. During Paint, visual properties such as colors, borders, and text are drawn. Finally, the Composite step combines layers and sends them to the GPU for display. Performance issues often arise from excessive reflows and repaints, so in modern React applications we optimize by minimizing DOM updates, batching state changes, and using GPU-accelerated properties like transform and opacity for animations.
content.interviewAnswer: The browser rendering pipeline converts HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into visible pixels. The browser first parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM. These are combined to create the Render Tree. Next, Layout (or Reflow) calculates element sizes and positions. During Paint, visual properties such as colors, borders, and text are drawn. Finally, the Composite step combines layers and sends them to the GPU for display. Performance issues often arise from excessive reflows and repaints, so in modern React applications we optimize by minimizing DOM updates, batching state changes, and using GPU-accelerated properties like transform and opacity for animations.

title: What Causes Memory Leaks in JavaScript?

content.overview: Common causes include global variables, unremoved event listeners, uncleared timers, detached DOM nodes, closures, unresolved async operations, and growing caches.
content.interviewAnswer: Common causes include global variables, unremoved event listeners, uncleared timers, detached DOM nodes, closures, unresolved async operations, and growing caches.

title: Web Vitals

content.overview: Web Vitals are performance metrics that measure real user experience. The three Core Web Vitals are LCP, INP, and CLS. LCP measures loading performance by tracking when the largest visible element renders. INP measures responsiveness by tracking how quickly the page reacts to user interactions. CLS measures visual stability by detecting unexpected layout shifts. In React applications, we improve Web Vitals through code splitting, lazy loading, image optimization, SSR, caching, virtualization, memoization, and reducing main-thread work. We monitor these metrics using the web-vitals package, Lighthouse, and Chrome DevTools to ensure a fast and stable user experience

title: Difference Between PUT and PATCH

content.overview: PUT replaces an entire resource. PATCH partially updates a resource.
content.interviewAnswer: PUT replaces an entire resource. PATCH partially updates a resource.

title: Promises vs try/catch

content.overview: Promises handle asynchronous operations. try/catch handles synchronous exceptions or async/await Promise rejections.
content.interviewAnswer: Promises handle asynchronous operations. try/catch handles synchronous exceptions or async/await Promise rejections.

title: slice() vs filter()

content.overview: slice() extracts elements by index. filter() returns elements matching a condition.
content.interviewAnswer: slice() extracts elements by index. filter() returns elements matching a condition.

title: Event Delegation, Bubbling and Capturing

content.overview: Event Delegation attaches one listener to a parent using event bubbling. Bubbling propagates upward. Capturing propagates downward.
content.interviewAnswer: Event Delegation attaches one listener to a parent using event bubbling. Bubbling propagates upward. Capturing propagates downward.

title: localStorage vs sessionStorage vs Cookies

content.overview: localStorage persists indefinitely, sessionStorage lasts per tab session, and cookies are sent with HTTP requests and are commonly used for authentication.
content.interviewAnswer: localStorage persists indefinitely, sessionStorage lasts per tab session, and cookies are sent with HTTP requests and are commonly used for authentication.

title: Web Workers vs Service Workers

content.overview: Web Workers perform CPU-intensive work off the main thread. Service Workers intercept network requests, enable caching, offline support, background sync, and push notifications.
content.interviewAnswer: Web Workers perform CPU-intensive work off the main thread. Service Workers intercept network requests, enable caching, offline support, background sync, and push notifications.

title: What is CORS?

content.overview: CORS allows servers to specify which origins may access resources using headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Complex requests require a preflight OPTIONS request.
content.interviewAnswer: CORS allows servers to specify which origins may access resources using headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Complex requests require a preflight OPTIONS request.

title: Explain React Data Flow in a Large App

content.overview: React follows one-way data flow where data moves from parent to child through props, and child components communicate changes upward through callbacks.
content.approach: Divide application state into local UI state, shared global state, server state, and URL state. Keep data ownership clear, avoid unnecessary prop drilling, and separate business logic from presentation using reusable hooks and selectors.
content.interviewAnswer: React follows one-way data flow, where data moves from parent to child through props, and child components communicate changes upward through callbacks. In a large application, I separate data into four categories: local UI state, shared global state, server state, and URL state. Local UI state stays within components, shared business state such as authentication or cart data is managed using Redux or Context, server state is handled using React Query or RTK Query for caching and synchronization, and filters or pagination are often stored in the URL. This architecture keeps data ownership clear, avoids unnecessary prop drilling, and makes the application scalable and maintainable.
keyPoints: Separate local, global, server, and URL state
Use selectors and custom hooks for reusable data access
examples: React Query for product API caching
URL query parameters for filters and pagination

title: How to Optimize a React Application?

content.overview: React performance is optimized by reducing unnecessary renders, minimizing bundle size, optimizing API requests, and improving rendering efficiency.
content.approach: Use memoization, state colocation, code splitting, lazy loading, virtualization, caching, debouncing, and performance monitoring tools.
content.interviewAnswer: I optimize React applications by reducing unnecessary re-renders using React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback. I optimize API calls using caching, debouncing, and efficient data fetching strategies. I implement code splitting and lazy loading to reduce the initial bundle size, and use virtualization for rendering large lists efficiently. I also follow state colocation by placing state as close as possible to where it is used, minimizing component re-renders. Finally, I monitor performance using Lighthouse and React DevTools to identify bottlenecks like large bundles and expensive renders.

title: How Do You Handle Authentication in React?

content.overview: Authentication is commonly implemented using access tokens, refresh tokens, protected routes, and centralized authentication state.
content.approach: Store authentication state centrally, attach access tokens to API requests, refresh expired tokens securely, and enforce authorization on the backend.
content.interviewAnswer: I usually implement authentication using access tokens and refresh tokens. After login, I store authentication state centrally, attach the access token to protected API requests, guard private routes, and refresh expired tokens automatically. For better security, I prefer storing the access token in memory and the refresh token inside an httpOnly cookie. I also separate authentication from authorization and ensure role-based access is validated by backend APIs.

title: How Do You Manage Global State in React?

content.overview: Global state should only contain shared client-side business data while server state should be managed separately.
content.approach: Separate client and server state, organize state by feature, normalize complex data, and use selectors to minimize coupling.
content.interviewAnswer: I avoid putting all application state into Redux. I separate client state from server state and organize Redux slices by feature rather than by data type. I use selectors to reduce coupling between components and normalize state when dealing with complex relationships. I always choose the simplest solution that scales well instead of introducing unnecessary global state.

title: Explain Modern React Architecture

content.overview: Modern React architecture focuses on feature-based organization, reusable custom hooks, and separation of concerns.
content.approach: Keep UI, state management, and API logic separated while extracting business logic into reusable hooks.
content.interviewAnswer: Instead of traditional container and presentational components, I prefer a hooks-based architecture where business logic is extracted into reusable custom hooks. I organize the application using a feature-based folder structure, keeping related components, APIs, hooks, and utilities together. I also separate UI, state management, and API logic into different layers, making the application scalable, maintainable, and easier to test.

title: How Do You Review Code?

content.overview: Effective code reviews ensure correctness, maintainability, performance, security, accessibility, and code quality.
content.approach: Review code layer by layer, provide constructive feedback, and rely on automated quality tools.
content.interviewAnswer: I review code by first verifying whether it satisfies the business requirement. Then I evaluate readability, architecture, edge cases, performance, security, accessibility, and testability. I provide constructive feedback that improves the code without blocking progress unnecessarily. I also rely on TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier, testing, CI pipelines, and regular refactoring to maintain consistent code quality.

title: What is Lazy Loading?

content.overview: Lazy loading is a performance optimization technique that loads components only when they are needed.
content.approach: Split code into smaller bundles using React.lazy() and Suspense to reduce the initial bundle size.
content.interviewAnswer: Lazy loading in React is a performance optimization technique where components are loaded only when needed instead of loading the entire application upfront. This reduces the initial bundle size and improves page load performance. React provides React.lazy() for dynamically importing components and Suspense for displaying fallback content while the component is loading.

title: Explain React Virtual DOM

content.overview: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM that helps React efficiently update the UI.
content.approach: React compares the previous and current Virtual DOM trees using reconciliation and updates only the changed DOM nodes.
content.interviewAnswer: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM. When state or props change, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and compares it with the previous one using its diffing algorithm. During reconciliation, React identifies the minimum set of changes and updates only those parts of the real DOM. Modern React uses the Fiber architecture to prioritize and schedule updates efficiently.

title: useState vs useReducer

content.overview: useState manages simple state while useReducer is better for complex state transitions.
content.approach: Choose useState for independent values and useReducer when multiple state values or business rules are related.
content.interviewAnswer: useState is ideal for simple, independent state values with straightforward updates. useReducer is preferred when state transitions become complex, multiple state values change together, or business logic needs to be centralized. I use useState for UI elements like modals, inputs, and toggles, while I use useReducer for shopping carts, multi-step forms, or complex workflows because it improves maintainability and testability.

title: Explain Props vs State

content.overview: Props are read-only values passed from parent to child, while state is mutable data managed within a component.
content.approach: Use props for component communication and state for managing changing data.
content.interviewAnswer: Props are read-only inputs passed from a parent component to a child component and are used for communication between components. State is data managed inside a component that changes over time. Whenever props or state change, React re-renders the component. If multiple components need the same state, I lift it to a common parent or manage it using Context or Redux.
keyPoints: Context or Redux for shared state

title: What is Context API?

content.overview: Context API is a built-in React feature that allows data to be shared across a component tree without manually passing props through every level.
content.approach: Create a Context object, wrap components with a Provider, and access shared values using the useContext hook.
content.interviewAnswer: Context API is a built-in React feature that allows data to be shared across a component tree without manually passing props through every level. It consists of a Context object, a Provider that supplies data, and consumers that access it using useContext. It is commonly used for themes, authentication, localization, and application settings. While it reduces prop drilling, updates to a Context value can trigger re-renders in consuming components, so for large-scale state management many teams combine Context with useReducer or use Redux Toolkit.

title: Explain React Performance Optimization

content.overview: React performance optimization focuses on minimizing unnecessary renders, reducing expensive computations, and improving application loading speed.
content.approach: Use memoization, lazy loading, virtualization, API caching, optimized Context usage, and performance profiling before applying optimizations.
content.interviewAnswer: React performance optimization focuses on minimizing unnecessary renders and reducing expensive operations. Common techniques include using React.memo for component memoization, useMemo for expensive calculations, and useCallback for stable function references. For large applications, I use route-based code splitting with React.lazy, virtualized lists with react-window, optimized Context usage, proper key management, and API caching with TanStack Query. I also rely on React DevTools Profiler and bundle analysis tools to identify actual bottlenecks before applying optimizations.

title: What's the First Thing You Do When a React App is Slow?

content.overview: Always profile first before optimizing to identify the real performance bottleneck.
content.approach: Use React DevTools Profiler and browser performance tools to determine whether the issue is rendering, networking, bundle size, or computation.
content.interviewAnswer: When a React application is slow, I profile first using React DevTools Profiler and browser performance tools. I avoid premature optimization and identify whether the bottleneck is caused by unnecessary re-renders, large lists, bundle size, slow network requests, or expensive computations before choosing solutions such as React.memo, useMemo, virtualization, or code splitting.

title: Class Component vs Functional Component

content.overview: Class Components use ES6 classes and lifecycle methods, while Functional Components use Hooks and are the modern React standard.
content.approach: Prefer Functional Components with Hooks for cleaner syntax, reusable logic, and better maintainability.
content.interviewAnswer: Class Components are ES6 classes that manage state using this.state and lifecycle methods such as componentDidMount and componentDidUpdate. Functional Components are plain JavaScript functions that use Hooks like useState and useEffect to manage state and side effects. Functional Components provide cleaner syntax, eliminate the need for this, support custom hooks for logic reuse, and are the recommended approach in modern React applications.

title: Explain Forms and Validation

content.overview: React forms are typically implemented using controlled components with validation performed on submit, blur, or input changes.
content.approach: Use useState for simple forms and React Hook Form with Zod for scalable, schema-based validation.
content.interviewAnswer: In React, forms are typically implemented using controlled components where input values are managed through state. Validation can be performed on submit, on blur, or in real time. For simple forms, useState is sufficient, but in production applications I prefer React Hook Form combined with Zod for schema-based validation. This approach improves performance by reducing unnecessary re-renders, provides better TypeScript support, and centralizes validation rules in reusable schemas.

title: What are React Hooks?

content.overview: React Hooks allow Functional Components to use state, lifecycle methods, context, refs, and other React features without Class Components.
content.approach: Use built-in Hooks for common functionality and Custom Hooks to reuse business logic across components.
content.interviewAnswer: React Hooks are functions that allow Functional Components to use React features such as state, lifecycle methods, context, refs, and side effects without writing Class Components. Common Hooks include useState for state management, useEffect for side effects, useContext for accessing Context, useRef for mutable references, and useMemo and useCallback for performance optimization. Hooks also enable logic reuse through Custom Hooks, which is one of the major architectural advantages of modern React development.

title: Explain React Router

content.overview: React Router is a client-side routing library that enables navigation between pages in a Single Page Application without full page reloads.
content.approach: Configure routes, support nested and dynamic routing, protect routes, and perform navigation using React Router v6 APIs.
content.interviewAnswer: React Router is a client-side routing library for React that enables navigation between views in a Single Page Application without full page reloads. It works by matching the current URL to configured routes and rendering the corresponding component. Key features include nested routes, dynamic route parameters, protected routes, query parameters, programmatic navigation using useNavigate, and lazy-loaded route-based code splitting. React Router v6 is the recommended version for modern applications.

title: What is SSR in Next.js?

content.overview: Server-Side Rendering (SSR) generates HTML on the server for every request before sending it to the browser.
content.approach: Use SSR for SEO-critical and dynamic pages requiring fresh data, then hydrate the page on the client.
content.interviewAnswer: SSR (Server-Side Rendering) in Next.js is a rendering strategy where HTML is generated on the server for every incoming request and sent to the browser. This improves SEO, initial page load performance, and content visibility because users receive fully rendered HTML before JavaScript executes. In the Pages Router, SSR is implemented using getServerSideProps, while in the App Router, Server Components provide SSR by default. After the HTML reaches the browser, React hydrates the page by attaching event handlers and making it interactive. SSR is ideal for SEO-critical and frequently changing content.

title: Explain getStaticProps vs getServerSideProps

content.overview: getStaticProps generates pages at build time, while getServerSideProps generates pages on every request.
content.approach: Choose getStaticProps for static content and getServerSideProps when fresh data is required for every request.
content.interviewAnswer: getStaticProps is used for Static Site Generation and runs at build time. The generated HTML is reused for all requests, making it extremely fast and suitable for content that changes infrequently, such as blogs and marketing pages. getServerSideProps is used for Server-Side Rendering and runs on every request, ensuring fresh data for each user. It is suitable for dynamic pages such as e-commerce product details, dashboards, and personalized content. The trade-off is that getStaticProps provides better performance, while getServerSideProps provides fresher data.

title: Explain REST vs GraphQL

content.overview: REST exposes multiple resource-based endpoints, whereas GraphQL exposes a single endpoint and lets clients request exactly the data they need.
content.approach: Choose REST for simple CRUD APIs and GraphQL for applications requiring flexible queries and complex relationships.
content.interviewAnswer: REST is an architectural style that exposes multiple resource-based endpoints and typically returns a fixed response structure. GraphQL is a query language and runtime that exposes a single endpoint and allows clients to request exactly the data they need. GraphQL solves over-fetching and under-fetching problems by enabling flexible queries and fetching related data in a single request. REST is simpler, easier to cache, and well-suited for straightforward CRUD operations, while GraphQL is ideal for applications with complex relationships, multiple clients, and dynamic data requirements.

title: API Calls and Error Handling in React

content.overview: API calls in React are typically performed using fetch, Axios, or data-fetching libraries like TanStack Query, with proper handling of loading, success, and error states.
content.approach: Centralize API logic in service layers, handle authentication using interceptors or middleware, and use TanStack Query for caching, retries, background synchronization, and error handling.
content.interviewAnswer: In React, API calls are typically made using fetch, Axios, or a data-fetching library such as TanStack Query. A robust implementation includes loading, success, and error states. Error handling should cover both network failures and HTTP response errors, since the Fetch API does not automatically throw for 4xx and 5xx responses. In production applications, I prefer centralizing API logic in service layers, handling authentication through interceptors or middleware, and using TanStack Query for caching, retries, background synchronization, and consistent error handling. This reduces boilerplate and improves maintainability and user experience.

title: Explain Authentication & Authorization

content.overview: Authentication verifies a user's identity, while Authorization determines what resources and actions that user is allowed to access.
content.approach: Authenticate users first, then apply role-based or permission-based authorization before granting access.
content.interviewAnswer: Authentication verifies the identity of a user (Who are you?), while Authorization determines what resources and actions that authenticated user is allowed to access (What can you do?). Authentication always happens first, followed by Authorization.

title: Where Would You Store JWT in a React Application?

content.overview: JWT tokens can be stored in HTTP-only cookies, Local Storage, or Session Storage, with HTTP-only cookies being the most secure option.
content.approach: Prefer storing access tokens in memory and refresh tokens in HTTP-only cookies to reduce XSS risks while maintaining a secure authentication flow.
content.interviewAnswer: The preferred approach is to use secure HTTP-only cookies because they are protected from JavaScript access and help prevent XSS attacks. Local Storage and Session Storage are simpler to implement but are more vulnerable to XSS. In enterprise applications, I prefer storing the access token in memory and the refresh token in an HTTP-only cookie using a refresh token strategy.

title: Explain Web Performance Optimization

content.overview: Web performance optimization focuses on improving loading speed, rendering performance, and user experience.
content.approach: Optimize rendering, bundle size, network delivery, and asset loading while continuously monitoring performance metrics.
content.interviewAnswer: In React and Next.js applications, I improve performance through code splitting, lazy loading, memoization (React.memo, useMemo, useCallback), image optimization, API caching, virtualization for large lists, and bundle-size reduction using tree shaking. I monitor performance using Lighthouse, Core Web Vitals, and Chrome DevTools. For production applications, I also use CDN caching, compression, and Next.js features like SSG, ISR, and dynamic imports to achieve faster load times and better user experience.

title: What is PWA?

content.overview: A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a web application that delivers a native app-like experience using modern web technologies.
content.approach: Use Service Workers, Web App Manifest, HTTPS, and caching to enable offline access, installation, and improved performance.
content.interviewAnswer: A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a web application that provides a native app-like experience using technologies such as Service Workers, Web App Manifest, HTTPS, and caching. PWAs support offline access, push notifications, installation from the browser, and responsive design, making them faster and more engaging than traditional web applications.

title: What is WCAG Accessibility?

content.overview: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) provides standards for building accessible web applications for all users, including people with disabilities.
content.approach: Use semantic HTML, keyboard accessibility, ARIA attributes, proper labels, sufficient color contrast, and accessibility testing tools.
content.interviewAnswer: In my React projects, I follow WCAG 2.1 AA standards by using semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, ARIA attributes, proper form labels, color contrast checks, focus management, and screen-reader-friendly components. I also use Lighthouse and axe DevTools to identify and fix accessibility issues before deployment.

title: What is Unit Testing?

content.overview: Unit Testing verifies that individual units of code such as functions, components, and hooks behave correctly in isolation.
content.approach: Write isolated tests using Jest and React Testing Library to validate rendering, business logic, and user interactions.
content.interviewAnswer: Unit Testing is the process of testing individual units of code such as functions, components, or hooks in isolation to ensure they behave correctly. In React applications, I typically use Jest and React Testing Library to test utility functions, custom hooks, component rendering, and user interactions. Unit tests help catch bugs early, improve maintainability, and provide confidence when refactoring code.

title: Explain Cypress vs Selenium

content.overview: Cypress and Selenium are browser automation frameworks used for end-to-end testing, but they differ in architecture and developer experience.
content.approach: Choose Cypress for modern frontend applications and Selenium when cross-browser, multi-language, or legacy browser support is required.
content.interviewAnswer: Selenium is a mature browser automation framework that uses WebDriver to interact with browsers and supports multiple programming languages. Cypress is a modern JavaScript-based testing framework that runs directly inside the browser, making it faster, easier to debug, and well-suited for React and modern frontend applications. For React projects, I generally prefer Cypress because of its automatic waiting, excellent debugging tools, API mocking capabilities, and simple setup.

title: Explain Git Workflow

content.overview: A feature-branch Git workflow enables parallel development, code reviews, and controlled releases.
content.approach: Create feature branches from develop, commit meaningful changes, open pull requests, perform code reviews, and merge into develop and main following release processes.
content.interviewAnswer: In my projects, I typically follow a feature-branch workflow. I create a feature branch from the develop branch, implement the feature, commit changes with meaningful commit messages, push the branch, and create a pull request. After code review and approval, the feature is merged into develop for QA testing and eventually merged into main for production deployment. I also regularly rebase or merge the latest develop branch to avoid conflicts and maintain a clean commit history.

title: How to Debug React Apps?

content.overview: Debugging React applications involves inspecting component state, network requests, rendering behavior, and production errors to identify root causes.
content.approach: Use browser developer tools, React DevTools, Redux DevTools, profiling tools, logging, and production monitoring platforms while following a systematic debugging process.
content.interviewAnswer: When debugging React applications, I typically start with Chrome DevTools and React Developer Tools to inspect component state, props, hooks, and network requests. For Redux applications, I use Redux DevTools to analyze state changes. I use breakpoints, console logging, and React Profiler to identify rendering and performance issues. In production environments, I rely on tools like Sentry and LogRocket for error monitoring and user-session analysis. My debugging approach focuses on isolating the issue, reproducing it consistently, identifying the root cause, and implementing a fix with proper testing.

title: What is Component-Driven Architecture?

content.overview: Component-Driven Architecture is a frontend design approach where applications are built from reusable, self-contained UI components.
content.approach: Build applications by composing reusable components that encapsulate their own UI, logic, styling, and behavior. Combine with Atomic Design and Storybook for scalable design systems.
content.interviewAnswer: Component-Driven Architecture is a frontend design approach where applications are built from reusable, self-contained UI components. Each component encapsulates its own logic, styling, and behavior, allowing developers to compose complex pages from smaller building blocks. In React projects, this approach improves reusability, scalability, maintainability, testing, and consistency across large applications. We often combine it with Atomic Design principles and Storybook to build scalable design systems.

title: How to Design a Complete Frontend Application?

content.overview: Designing a frontend application involves creating a scalable architecture, organizing features, optimizing performance, ensuring accessibility, testing thoroughly, and supporting production deployment.
content.approach: Use a feature-based architecture, Component-Driven Design, service layers, Redux Toolkit, custom hooks, performance optimizations, accessibility standards, testing frameworks, CI/CD pipelines, and monitoring tools.
content.interviewAnswer: When designing a frontend application, I start by understanding business requirements and defining a scalable architecture. I use a feature-based structure with reusable components following Component-Driven Architecture. I separate presentation, business logic, API services, and state management. For global state, I typically use Redux Toolkit, while API interactions are abstracted through service layers and custom hooks. I ensure performance through code splitting, lazy loading, memoization, and image optimization. Accessibility is implemented according to WCAG standards, and testing is covered through Jest, React Testing Library, and Cypress. Finally, CI/CD pipelines using GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, or Jenkins, along with monitoring tools such as Sentry and LogRocket, support production-grade deployments.

title: What is React and Why is it Efficient?

content.overview: React is a JavaScript library for building dynamic and reusable user interfaces. It is efficient because it minimizes expensive DOM updates using the Virtual DOM and Fiber architecture.
content.approach: React creates a Virtual DOM, compares updates using reconciliation, and efficiently updates only changed parts of the Real DOM while leveraging component reuse and modern rendering optimizations.
content.interviewAnswer: React is a JavaScript library used to build dynamic and reusable user interfaces. It is efficient because it uses a Virtual DOM, which creates a lightweight representation of the actual DOM. When state changes, React updates the Virtual DOM, compares it with the previous version using the reconciliation algorithm, and updates only the changed elements in the real DOM. React also improves performance through component reusability, one-way data flow, batched state updates, React Fiber architecture, and optimization techniques like React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback. These features make React highly performant and scalable for large applications.

title: How Does React Work Internally?

content.overview: React internally converts JSX into React elements, builds a Virtual DOM, performs reconciliation using Fiber, and efficiently updates the Real DOM.
content.approach: React creates a work-in-progress Virtual DOM tree, compares it with the current tree, schedules updates using Fiber, and commits only the necessary DOM changes.
content.interviewAnswer: Internally, React converts JSX into React elements and builds a Virtual DOM tree. Modern React uses the Fiber architecture, where every component is represented as a Fiber node. When state or props change, React schedules an update, creates a new Virtual DOM tree, and performs reconciliation by comparing it with the previous tree. The diffing algorithm identifies the minimum set of changes needed. During the commit phase, React updates only the affected DOM nodes rather than re-rendering the entire page. React Fiber also enables prioritization, interruptible rendering, batching, and concurrent features, which significantly improve performance and user experience in large applications.

title: Virtual DOM vs Real DOM

content.overview: The Real DOM is the browser's actual document structure, while the Virtual DOM is React's lightweight JavaScript representation used for efficient updates.
content.approach: React compares Virtual DOM trees and updates only the necessary Real DOM nodes, reducing expensive DOM operations.
content.interviewAnswer: The Real DOM is the actual browser representation of a web page, and updating it is expensive because it can trigger layout recalculations and repainting. React uses a Virtual DOM, which is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the UI. When state or props change, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and compares it with the previous one using its reconciliation algorithm. It identifies the minimum set of changes required and updates only those parts of the Real DOM. This reduces costly DOM operations, improves rendering performance, and enables React applications to scale efficiently.
examples: Updating one list item instead of the entire list

title: What is Reconciliation?

content.overview: Reconciliation is React's process of comparing Virtual DOM trees and updating only the necessary parts of the Real DOM.
content.approach: React compares the previous and current Virtual DOM trees using heuristics and keys to determine the minimal DOM updates.
content.interviewAnswer: Reconciliation is React's process of updating the UI efficiently when state or props change. React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and compares it with the previous Virtual DOM using its diffing algorithm. Based on a set of heuristics, React identifies the minimum set of changes required and updates only those parts of the Real DOM. If element types differ, React replaces the subtree; if they are the same, it updates only changed attributes or content. Keys play a crucial role in efficiently reconciling lists. Modern React uses the Fiber architecture to make reconciliation interruptible, prioritized, and more performant for large applications.

title: Explain React Fiber Architecture

content.overview: React Fiber is React's reconciliation engine that enables scheduling, prioritization, interruptible rendering, and concurrent features.
content.approach: Represent each component as a Fiber node, perform reconciliation during the render phase, and apply DOM updates during the commit phase.
content.interviewAnswer: React Fiber is the reconciliation engine introduced in React 16. It replaces the old synchronous stack reconciler with an architecture that represents each component as a Fiber node. Fiber allows React to break rendering work into small units, assign priorities, pause and resume rendering, and schedule updates efficiently. React maintains a current Fiber tree and a work-in-progress Fiber tree. During the render phase, React performs reconciliation and computes changes, while during the commit phase it applies updates to the DOM. Fiber is the foundation for modern React features such as Concurrent Rendering, Suspense, Transitions, automatic batching, and improved responsiveness in large applications.

title: Why are Keys Important in React?

content.overview: Keys uniquely identify elements in a list and help React efficiently reconcile UI updates.
content.approach: Always use stable, unique identifiers instead of array indexes for dynamic lists.
content.interviewAnswer: Keys are unique identifiers used by React to track elements in a list during reconciliation. When a list changes due to insertion, deletion, or reordering, React uses keys to determine which items have changed, been added, or been removed. This allows React to reuse existing DOM nodes and component instances efficiently instead of recreating them. Using stable unique keys improves performance, preserves component state, and prevents rendering bugs. Using array indexes as keys is generally discouraged for dynamic lists because indexes change when items are added, removed, or reordered, leading to incorrect UI behavior and unnecessary re-renders.

title: useMemo vs useCallback vs React.memo

content.overview: React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback are optimization techniques that prevent unnecessary rendering and computation.
content.approach: Use React.memo for components, useMemo for computed values, and useCallback for function references.
content.interviewAnswer: React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback are React optimization tools but serve different purposes. React.memo memoizes an entire component and prevents re-renders when props haven't changed. useMemo memoizes the result of an expensive computation and recomputes it only when dependencies change. useCallback memoizes a function reference, preventing unnecessary function recreation and reducing child component re-renders when callbacks are passed as props. They are often used together: React.memo for component-level optimization, useMemo for value-level optimization, and useCallback for function-level optimization.

title: When Should You Avoid useMemo?

content.overview: Avoid useMemo for inexpensive computations because memoization itself introduces overhead.
content.approach: Reserve useMemo for expensive calculations or when referential equality is required for optimization.
content.interviewAnswer: Avoid useMemo for inexpensive computations because the memoization itself has a cost. It should be reserved for expensive calculations or when maintaining referential equality is necessary for child component optimizations. Overusing useMemo can actually reduce performance and increase code complexity, so it should be applied only after profiling demonstrates a real performance bottleneck.

title: How Does React.memo Compare Props?

content.overview: React.memo prevents unnecessary component re-renders by performing a shallow comparison of props using Object.is.
content.approach: React compares each prop individually. Primitive values are compared by value, while objects, arrays, and functions are compared by reference.
content.interviewAnswer: React.memo performs a shallow comparison using Object.is on each prop. Primitive values such as strings, numbers, and booleans are compared by value, while objects, arrays, and functions are compared by reference. If all props are considered equal, React skips re-rendering the component. Otherwise, the component re-renders.

title: Why Does a Child Re-render When a Callback Prop Changes?

content.overview: A child component re-renders because a new callback function reference is created on every parent render.
content.approach: Memoize callback functions using useCallback when passing them to memoized child components.
content.interviewAnswer: A callback prop causes re-renders because a new function object is created on every render. Since React.memo performs a shallow comparison, it detects that the callback reference has changed and re-renders the child component. The useCallback hook can stabilize the function reference so the child only re-renders when its dependencies actually change.

title: What Is Referential Equality in React?

content.overview: Referential equality means two values point to the same memory location, and React relies on it to detect changes.
content.approach: Maintain stable references when necessary using useMemo and useCallback to avoid unnecessary renders.
content.interviewAnswer: Referential equality means two values reference the same memory location. React uses referential equality to determine whether props, state, dependency values, or callback references have changed. When a new object, array, or function is created, its reference changes even if the contents are identical, which can trigger unnecessary re-renders.

title: Can useCallback Replace useMemo?

content.overview: No. useMemo memoizes computed values, whereas useCallback memoizes function references.
content.approach: Use useMemo for expensive calculations and useCallback for stable callback references.
content.interviewAnswer: No. useMemo memoizes values, whereas useCallback memoizes function references. Although useCallback is internally similar to useMemo(() => fn, deps), their intended use cases are different. Use useMemo for expensive computations and useCallback when passing callbacks to child components or dependency arrays.

title: What Are the Drawbacks of Excessive Memoization?

content.overview: Overusing memoization can negatively impact performance and code maintainability.
content.approach: Only memoize when profiling demonstrates measurable performance improvements.
content.interviewAnswer: Excessive memoization increases memory usage, adds dependency tracking overhead, and makes code harder to read and maintain. Since memoization itself has a cost, it should only be applied when profiling shows a measurable performance benefit instead of being used everywhere by default.

title: How Do You Profile React Performance?

content.overview: React performance should be profiled before optimization to identify real bottlenecks.
content.approach: Use React DevTools Profiler, Chrome Performance tools, and rendering highlights to analyze rendering behavior.
content.interviewAnswer: I primarily use React DevTools Profiler to identify unnecessary renders and measure render durations. I also use Chrome Performance tools and highlight updates to understand rendering bottlenecks before applying optimizations. This ensures performance improvements target actual issues rather than relying on guesswork.

title: What Happens If Hook Dependencies Are Incorrect?

content.overview: Incorrect dependency arrays can cause stale values, missed updates, unnecessary renders, or infinite loops.
content.approach: Always specify correct dependencies and rely on the React Hooks ESLint plugin to detect mistakes.
content.interviewAnswer: Incorrect dependencies can lead to stale closures, stale values, missed updates, unnecessary re-renders, or infinite loops. The React Hooks ESLint plugin helps catch dependency issues by warning when required dependencies are missing or unnecessary.

title: How Does React.memo Work with Context API?

content.overview: React.memo only optimizes prop changes. Context updates bypass React.memo and re-render all consuming components.
content.approach: Optimize Context using context splitting, memoized values, or selector-based state management.
content.interviewAnswer: React.memo only optimizes prop changes. Context updates bypass React.memo and trigger re-renders for every component consuming that context. To improve performance, I split contexts by responsibility, memoize provider values, or use selector-based state management libraries that minimize unnecessary updates.

title: What Optimizations Would You Apply in a Large E-commerce Product List?

content.overview: Large product lists require rendering, data-fetching, and interaction optimizations to provide a smooth user experience.
content.approach: Profile first, then apply virtualization, memoization, API caching, lazy loading, pagination, and concurrent rendering where appropriate.
content.interviewAnswer: For a large e-commerce product list, I would first profile the application using React DevTools to identify actual bottlenecks. I would then use virtualization to render only visible items, React.memo for product cards, useMemo for filtering and sorting, useCallback for stable event handlers, lazy loading for images and components, API caching with TanStack Query, pagination or infinite scrolling, and React 18 concurrent features such as startTransition to keep the UI responsive.

title: Explain React Rendering Lifecycle

content.overview: React's rendering lifecycle consists of Mounting, Updating, and Unmounting, with internal Render and Commit phases managed by the Fiber architecture.
content.approach: React schedules updates, performs reconciliation during the Render phase, commits DOM changes during the Commit phase, and executes effect cleanup and lifecycle logic appropriately.
content.interviewAnswer: React's rendering lifecycle consists of Mounting, Updating, and Unmounting phases. During mounting, React executes the component, builds the Virtual DOM and Fiber tree, performs the Render phase, commits DOM updates, and then runs effects. During updates triggered by state, props, or context changes, React schedules work, performs reconciliation by comparing Virtual DOM trees, commits the necessary DOM changes, and executes effect cleanups followed by new effects. During unmounting, React runs cleanup functions and removes DOM nodes. Internally, React separates work into a Render Phase, where changes are calculated, and a Commit Phase, where changes are applied. Modern React Fiber allows rendering work to be paused, resumed, and prioritized for better responsiveness.

title: Explain useEffect Dependency Array

content.overview: The dependency array in useEffect controls when an effect executes by tracking changes in specified dependencies.
content.approach: Provide the correct dependency array so React can synchronize effects efficiently while avoiding stale closures, unnecessary executions, and infinite loops.
content.interviewAnswer: The dependency array in useEffect controls when an effect executes. React compares each dependency with its previous value using Object.is. Without a dependency array, the effect runs after every render. An empty array causes the effect to run only after the initial mount. When dependencies are specified, the effect runs on mount and whenever any dependency changes. Correct dependency management is essential to avoid stale closures, infinite loops, unnecessary re-executions, and synchronization bugs. Functions and objects often require useCallback or useMemo to maintain stable references when used as dependencies.

title: What Happens If You Omit the Dependency Array?

content.overview: Omitting the dependency array causes the effect to execute after every render.
content.approach: Only omit the dependency array when the effect genuinely needs to run after every render.
content.interviewAnswer: Omitting the dependency array causes useEffect to run after every render, including the initial render and all subsequent re-renders. This is useful only in rare cases because it can negatively impact performance or even lead to infinite loops if the effect updates state.

title: What Is a Stale Closure?

content.overview: A stale closure occurs when a hook captures outdated values from a previous render due to missing dependencies.
content.approach: Always include all referenced values in the dependency array to keep effects synchronized with the latest state and props.
content.interviewAnswer: A stale closure occurs when a hook captures outdated values from a previous render because required dependencies are missing. As a result, the effect continues to use stale state or props even after they have changed. The exhaustive-deps ESLint rule helps prevent this issue.

title: Why Do Functions Cause Effects to Rerun?

content.overview: Functions trigger effect re-execution because React compares function references rather than function contents.
content.approach: Use useCallback to stabilize function references when they are dependencies.
content.interviewAnswer: Functions cause effects to rerun because React compares dependencies by reference. A new function object is created on every render unless it is memoized with useCallback. Since the reference changes, React considers the dependency changed and re-executes the effect.

title: Why Do Objects Cause Effects to Rerun?

content.overview: Objects trigger effect re-execution because React compares object references instead of deeply comparing object values.
content.approach: Memoize objects using useMemo or move object creation outside the component when appropriate.
content.interviewAnswer: Objects cause effects to rerun because React compares references rather than deep object values. Every newly created object has a different reference even if its contents are identical. Memoizing objects with useMemo helps maintain stable references.

title: What Is the exhaustive-deps ESLint Rule?

content.overview: The exhaustive-deps ESLint rule ensures hook dependency arrays include all referenced values.
content.approach: Follow the rule to prevent stale closures and inconsistent application behavior.
content.interviewAnswer: The exhaustive-deps ESLint rule ensures that every value referenced inside a hook callback is included in its dependency array. This reduces bugs caused by stale closures, missed updates, and inconsistent state synchronization.

title: When Does the Cleanup Function Run?

content.overview: Cleanup functions release resources before an effect re-executes or when a component unmounts.
content.approach: Return a cleanup function from useEffect to remove subscriptions, timers, or event listeners.
content.interviewAnswer: Cleanup functions run before an effect re-executes due to dependency changes and when the component unmounts. They are commonly used to remove event listeners, cancel timers, unsubscribe from services, or abort ongoing requests to prevent memory leaks.

title: Can useEffect Cause Infinite Loops?

content.overview: Yes. Incorrect dependency management can cause effects to continuously trigger re-renders.
content.approach: Avoid updating state inside an effect when that same state directly triggers the effect unless necessary.
content.interviewAnswer: Yes. Infinite loops occur when an effect updates a state that is included in its own dependency array, causing continuous re-renders. They can also occur when unstable objects or functions are used as dependencies. Proper dependency management and memoization help prevent these issues.

title: How Does React Compare Dependencies?

content.overview: React compares dependencies using Object.is to determine whether an effect should re-execute.
content.approach: Maintain stable references for objects, arrays, and functions when using them as dependencies.
content.interviewAnswer: React compares dependencies using Object.is. Primitive values such as strings and numbers are compared by value, while objects, arrays, and functions are compared by reference. If any dependency changes according to Object.is, React re-executes the effect.

title: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect

content.overview: useEffect runs after the browser paints, while useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM updates but before painting.
content.approach: Use useEffect for most side effects and reserve useLayoutEffect for DOM measurements or layout calculations that must happen before paint.
content.interviewAnswer: useEffect runs asynchronously after the browser paints the UI, making it suitable for most side effects such as data fetching, subscriptions, and logging. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before the browser paints, making it useful for DOM measurements, layout calculations, or preventing visual flickering. Because useLayoutEffect blocks painting, it should be used only when necessary.

title: Why Should You Avoid Suppressing Dependency Warnings?

content.overview: Suppressing dependency warnings can hide stale closures and synchronization bugs in React Hooks.
content.approach: Instead of disabling warnings, refactor the effect or stabilize dependencies using useMemo or useCallback.
content.interviewAnswer: Suppressing dependency warnings can hide stale closures and synchronization bugs. The warning usually indicates that the effect depends on a value that may change. Instead of suppressing it, the effect should be refactored or dependencies should be stabilized using useMemo or useCallback. Following the exhaustive-deps rule leads to more predictable and maintainable code.

title: Why Should useEffect Callback Not Be Async?

content.overview: The callback passed to useEffect must return either nothing or a cleanup function, not a Promise.
content.approach: Create an async function inside the effect and invoke it synchronously to perform asynchronous work.
content.interviewAnswer: The callback passed to useEffect should not be async because React expects the effect function to return either nothing or a cleanup function. Async functions always return a Promise, which React cannot use as a cleanup handler. To perform asynchronous operations, the recommended pattern is to define an async function inside the effect and invoke it synchronously. This design also helps React manage cleanup logic predictably and avoids issues related to race conditions, memory leaks, and state updates after component unmounting.

title: How Does React Handle State Updates?

content.overview: React schedules state updates using its Fiber architecture instead of updating state immediately.
content.approach: React creates update objects, stores them in an update queue, schedules rendering based on priority, performs reconciliation, and commits only the necessary DOM changes.
content.interviewAnswer: React handles state updates by creating update objects and placing them into an update queue associated with a component's Fiber node. Instead of updating state immediately, React schedules the update using its Fiber scheduler, assigns a priority, and performs rendering asynchronously when appropriate. During the render phase, React processes queued updates, computes the new state, generates a new Virtual DOM tree, and performs reconciliation. During the commit phase, React applies the minimal DOM changes. React 18 further optimizes this process with automatic batching and concurrent rendering, allowing updates to be prioritized and processed efficiently.

title: Why Are State Updates Asynchronous?

content.overview: React schedules state updates asynchronously to improve rendering performance and responsiveness.
content.approach: Batch multiple updates, prioritize rendering work, and minimize unnecessary re-renders.
content.interviewAnswer: State updates are asynchronous because React schedules updates rather than applying them immediately. This allows React to batch multiple updates, prioritize work, reduce unnecessary renders, and improve application performance. The asynchronous scheduling model is a key part of React's Fiber architecture.
examples: Multiple state updates in one event

title: What Is Batching in React?

content.overview: Batching is React's optimization that groups multiple state updates into a single render cycle.
content.approach: Combine related state updates before rendering to reduce unnecessary re-renders.
content.interviewAnswer: Batching is React's optimization technique where multiple state updates are grouped together and processed in a single render cycle. This minimizes unnecessary renders and improves application performance by reducing the number of DOM updates.
examples: Multiple setState calls in one click handler

title: What Is Automatic Batching in React 18?

content.overview: React 18 automatically batches state updates across synchronous and asynchronous boundaries.
content.approach: Allow React to batch updates from promises, timeouts, and native events to reduce unnecessary rendering.
content.interviewAnswer: React 18 introduced automatic batching, which batches state updates across all asynchronous boundaries such as promises, timeouts, and native event handlers. This reduces unnecessary renders and improves overall application performance without requiring developers to manually optimize update grouping.

title: Why Use Functional Updates?

content.overview: Functional updates ensure state calculations always use the latest available state.
content.approach: Pass a callback to the state setter whenever the next state depends on the previous state.
content.interviewAnswer: Functional updates ensure that each state update uses the latest state value, avoiding stale state issues when multiple updates are queued. Instead of relying on the current closure value, React provides the latest state as an argument to the updater function.

title: How Does React Schedule Updates?

content.overview: React schedules updates using the Fiber scheduler, which assigns priorities and processes rendering work efficiently.
content.approach: React prioritizes updates based on urgency, allowing less important rendering work to be paused or deferred.
content.interviewAnswer: React schedules updates through the Fiber scheduler. Updates are assigned priorities and processed according to urgency, allowing React to keep the UI responsive. This scheduling system enables interruptible rendering, concurrent features, automatic batching, and smoother user interactions in large applications.

title: What Is an Update Queue?

content.overview: An update queue is React's internal data structure that stores pending state updates before rendering.
content.approach: React accumulates update objects in a queue and processes them during the next render cycle.
content.interviewAnswer: An update queue is an internal data structure used by React to store pending state updates until they are processed during the next render cycle. Each update is represented as an update object, allowing React to batch, prioritize, and process multiple updates efficiently.

title: What Happens After setState()?

content.overview: Calling setState schedules a state update that passes through React's update queue, render phase, reconciliation, and commit phase.
content.approach: React creates an update object, queues it, schedules rendering, computes the new Virtual DOM, performs reconciliation, and commits only the required DOM updates.
content.interviewAnswer: After setState is called, React creates an update object, places it in the component's update queue, schedules rendering, processes the update during the render phase, performs reconciliation, and finally updates the DOM during the commit phase. Because updates are scheduled rather than applied immediately, React can batch multiple updates and optimize rendering performance.

title: What is the Difference Between Render Phase and Commit Phase?

content.overview: React separates rendering into a Render Phase, where changes are calculated, and a Commit Phase, where those changes are applied to the DOM.
content.approach: During rendering React builds a work-in-progress Fiber tree and performs reconciliation. During commit React updates the DOM, assigns refs, and executes effects.
content.interviewAnswer: During the render phase React computes what should change by creating a new Fiber tree and reconciling it with the previous one. This phase is pure and may be paused, resumed, or restarted by the Fiber scheduler. During the commit phase React applies those changes to the DOM, updates refs, executes layout effects, paints the UI, and then runs passive effects such as useEffect. Unlike the render phase, the commit phase is synchronous and cannot be interrupted.

title: How Does React Fiber Manage State Updates?

content.overview: React Fiber stores component state and pending updates on Fiber nodes and schedules rendering based on priority.
content.approach: React attaches updates to Fiber nodes, assigns priority lanes, builds a work-in-progress tree, performs reconciliation, and commits changes.
content.interviewAnswer: React Fiber stores state and pending updates on Fiber nodes. When a state update occurs, React attaches the update to the Fiber, assigns a priority lane, builds a work-in-progress tree, processes queued updates during the render phase, performs reconciliation, and commits the result when rendering completes. This architecture enables interruptible rendering, prioritization, batching, and concurrent features.

title: How Does startTransition() Affect Update Priority?

content.overview: startTransition marks updates as non-urgent so React prioritizes user interactions before expensive rendering work.
content.approach: Wrap non-urgent updates inside startTransition so urgent updates such as typing remain responsive.
content.interviewAnswer: startTransition marks updates as non-urgent. React assigns them a lower-priority lane, allowing urgent updates such as typing, clicking, or input changes to be processed first. This improves responsiveness in scenarios involving expensive rendering, filtering, sorting, or large UI updates. React may pause, delay, or restart transition updates if higher-priority work arrives.

title: Explain Redux Architecture

content.overview: Redux is a predictable state management library that stores application state in a centralized store using unidirectional data flow.
content.approach: Dispatch actions, process them in reducers, update immutable state, and access state through selectors.
content.interviewAnswer: Redux is a predictable state management library that maintains application state in a centralized store. Components dispatch actions describing what happened, reducers process those actions and return new immutable state, and the store updates accordingly. Redux follows a unidirectional data flow where state changes are predictable and traceable. Modern Redux applications typically use Redux Toolkit, which simplifies store configuration, reducer creation, immutable updates, and async operations through createSlice and createAsyncThunk. This architecture improves scalability, maintainability, debugging, and state consistency in large applications.

title: What is Redux Toolkit (RTK)?

content.overview: Redux Toolkit is the official Redux package that simplifies Redux development and follows Redux best practices.
content.approach: Use configureStore, createSlice, createAsyncThunk, and Immer to reduce boilerplate and improve developer productivity.
content.interviewAnswer: Redux Toolkit is the official Redux package that simplifies Redux development by providing createSlice, configureStore, createAsyncThunk, and Immer integration. It reduces boilerplate, improves developer experience, and follows Redux best practices.

title: Why Must Reducers Be Pure Functions?

content.overview: Reducers must be pure so Redux state updates remain predictable and testable.
content.approach: Always return new state based only on current state and action without side effects.
content.interviewAnswer: Reducers must be pure functions because Redux depends on predictable state transitions. Pure reducers make debugging, testing, state tracking, and time-travel debugging possible.

title: What Is Immutability in Redux?

content.overview: Immutability means creating new state instead of modifying existing state directly.
content.approach: Always return a new state object so Redux can detect changes through reference comparisons.
content.interviewAnswer: Immutability means never modifying existing state directly. Instead, a new state object is created. This enables Redux to efficiently detect changes using reference comparisons and ensures predictable state updates.

title: What Is Middleware in Redux?

content.overview: Middleware intercepts dispatched actions before they reach reducers.
content.approach: Use middleware for asynchronous logic, logging, analytics, and handling side effects.
content.interviewAnswer: Middleware intercepts dispatched actions before they reach reducers. It is commonly used for asynchronous logic, logging, analytics, authentication, and side-effect management.

title: How Does Redux Thunk Work?

content.overview: Redux Thunk enables asynchronous logic by allowing action creators to return functions.
content.approach: Dispatch asynchronous operations before dispatching regular Redux actions.
content.interviewAnswer: Redux Thunk is middleware that allows action creators to return functions instead of plain objects. These functions receive dispatch and getState, enabling asynchronous operations before dispatching actions.

title: What is createAsyncThunk?

content.overview: createAsyncThunk simplifies asynchronous Redux logic by automatically generating lifecycle actions.
content.approach: Return a promise and handle pending, fulfilled, and rejected states in reducers.
content.interviewAnswer: createAsyncThunk is a Redux Toolkit utility for handling asynchronous logic. It automatically dispatches pending, fulfilled, and rejected actions based on the promise lifecycle.

title: Redux vs Context API
