content.overview: Redux is designed for scalable application state management, while Context API is intended for lightweight shared state.
content.approach: Use Context for simple global values and Redux for complex application state requiring middleware and debugging tools.
content.interviewAnswer: Context API is suitable for lightweight global state such as themes or authentication, while Redux provides advanced features like middleware, DevTools, normalized state management, and better scalability for large applications.

title: How Does useSelector Trigger Re-renders?

content.overview: useSelector subscribes to the Redux store and re-renders only when the selected value changes.
content.approach: Keep selectors focused and memoized when necessary to reduce unnecessary re-renders.
content.interviewAnswer: useSelector subscribes to the Redux store and re-executes its selector whenever the store changes. If the selected value changes according to strict reference comparison, React re-renders the component.

title: Why Should the State Not Be Mutated?

content.overview: Redux relies on immutable state updates to detect changes efficiently.
content.approach: Always create new state objects instead of modifying existing ones.
content.interviewAnswer: State should not be mutated because Redux relies on immutable updates and reference comparisons to detect changes. Mutating state can lead to missed updates, unpredictable behavior, and debugging difficulties.

title: How Does Redux DevTools Work?

content.overview: Redux DevTools records dispatched actions and state transitions for debugging.
content.approach: Inspect actions, compare state changes, replay actions, and perform time-travel debugging.
content.interviewAnswer: Redux DevTools intercepts dispatched actions and records the previous and next application state. It enables debugging, state inspection, action replay, and time-travel debugging by maintaining a history of state transitions.

title: Explain JWT Authentication Flow

content.overview: JWT authentication is a stateless authentication mechanism using signed JSON Web Tokens.
content.approach: Authenticate the user, issue access and refresh tokens, validate tokens on protected requests, and refresh expired access tokens securely.
content.interviewAnswer: JWT authentication is a stateless authentication mechanism where a user logs in with credentials, the server validates them, and generates a signed JSON Web Token containing user claims. The client stores the token and includes it in subsequent requests, typically in the Authorization header as a Bearer token. The server verifies the token's signature and expiration before granting access to protected resources. Modern implementations typically use short-lived access tokens and long-lived refresh tokens, with HttpOnly secure cookies for improved security. JWTs improve scalability because authentication state is stored on the client rather than the server.

title: Different Approaches for API Handling

content.overview: React supports multiple API handling strategies depending on application complexity and state management requirements.
content.approach: Choose fetch or Axios for simple applications, Redux Toolkit for shared async state, and TanStack Query for scalable server-state management.
content.interviewAnswer: There are several approaches to API handling in React, ranging from native fetch and Axios to advanced solutions such as Redux Toolkit, TanStack Query, SWR, and GraphQL clients. For small applications, Axios combined with custom hooks provides a clean architecture. For globally shared server state, Redux Toolkit with createAsyncThunk is common. For modern scalable applications, TanStack Query is often preferred because it provides built-in caching, background synchronization, retries, request deduplication, and loading/error state management. In production systems, API calls are usually abstracted into service layers and integrated with authentication, interceptors, and centralized error handling.

title: Explain React Portals

content.overview: React Portals render DOM elements outside their parent DOM hierarchy while remaining part of the same React component tree.
content.approach: Use ReactDOM.createPortal to render overlays that need to escape layout or stacking constraints.
content.interviewAnswer: React Portals allow components to render their DOM elements outside their parent DOM hierarchy while remaining part of the same React component tree. They are created using ReactDOM.createPortal and are commonly used for modals, dialogs, tooltips, dropdowns, and overlays that need to escape CSS constraints such as overflow, z-index, or stacking contexts. Although the DOM location changes, React features such as context, state, hooks, refs, and event bubbling continue to work normally because the component remains in the same React tree.

title: Redux Toolkit vs TanStack Query

content.overview: Redux Toolkit manages client state, while TanStack Query manages server state and caching.
content.approach: Use Redux Toolkit for application state and TanStack Query for API data synchronization and caching.
content.interviewAnswer: Redux Toolkit manages client state such as authentication, UI state, and business logic, while TanStack Query manages server state by handling data fetching, caching, synchronization, retries, and background updates. In many production applications, both libraries are used together because they solve different problems.

title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components

content.overview: Controlled components are managed by React state, while uncontrolled components store values in the DOM.
content.approach: Use controlled components for predictable state management and validation, and uncontrolled components when optimizing large forms.
content.interviewAnswer: A controlled component is a form element whose value is managed by React state using useState. React becomes the single source of truth, making validation, conditional rendering, and state management easier. An uncontrolled component stores its value in the DOM and is accessed using useRef. React does not track every change, resulting in fewer re-renders and potentially better performance. In most React applications, I prefer controlled components because they provide better predictability and validation. For large forms or libraries like React Hook Form, uncontrolled components are often used internally for performance optimization.

title: Hydration in Next.js and UI Mismatches

content.overview: Hydration attaches React's client-side logic to server-rendered HTML. Mismatches occur when client-rendered output differs from server-rendered HTML.
content.approach: Keep server output deterministic, move browser-only logic to useEffect, use Client Components when required, and dynamically import browser-only libraries.
content.interviewAnswer: Hydration in Next.js is the process where React attaches event handlers and client-side logic to the HTML that was pre-rendered on the server, making the application interactive. A hydration mismatch occurs when the HTML generated on the server differs from what React renders on the client during hydration. Common causes include using Date, Math.random, window, document, localStorage, or browser-specific logic during rendering. To avoid hydration issues, keep server-rendered output deterministic, move browser-only logic into useEffect, use Client Components when necessary, and dynamically import browser-only libraries with ssr: false. These practices help prevent hydration warnings and UI flickering.

title: CSR vs SSR vs SSG

content.overview: CSR, SSR, and SSG are different rendering strategies in Next.js, each optimized for different use cases involving SEO, performance, and data freshness.
content.approach: Choose the rendering strategy based on application requirements. Use CSR for highly interactive authenticated applications, SSR for dynamic SEO-sensitive pages, and SSG/ISR for static public content.
content.interviewAnswer: CSR, SSR, and SSG are different rendering strategies in Next.js. CSR (Client-Side Rendering) renders the page in the browser using JavaScript. It's suitable for highly interactive applications like dashboards but is weaker for SEO. SSR (Server-Side Rendering) generates HTML on the server for every request, providing fresh data and excellent SEO, making it ideal for e-commerce and dynamic content. SSG (Static Site Generation) generates HTML at build time and serves static files through a CDN. It offers the best performance and SEO and is commonly used for blogs, documentation, and marketing pages. In modern Next.js applications, I typically use SSG/ISR for public content, SSR for dynamic SEO-sensitive pages, and CSR for authenticated dashboards and highly interactive features.

title: How Would You Design a Scalable React App With 100+ Pages?

content.overview: Large React applications require a scalable architecture, modular organization, performance optimization, and maintainable development practices.
content.approach: Adopt feature-based architecture, reusable components, centralized API services, state management, testing, CI/CD, and performance optimization techniques.
content.interviewAnswer: For a React application with 100+ pages, I would use a feature-based architecture, reusable design system, Redux Toolkit for global state, React Query for server state, route-level code splitting, role-based routing, centralized API services, comprehensive testing, and CI/CD automation. I would also optimize performance using lazy loading, memoization, and virtualization, ensuring the application remains maintainable, scalable, and performant as multiple teams contribute to the codebase.

title: How Would You Build a Component Library Used by Multiple Teams?

content.overview: A shared component library improves UI consistency, developer productivity, and maintainability across multiple applications.
content.approach: Build reusable, accessible, TypeScript-based components documented in Storybook with automated testing, semantic versioning, and CI/CD.
content.interviewAnswer: I would build a centralized component library backed by a design system and design tokens. Components would be reusable, accessible, fully typed with TypeScript, documented in Storybook, tested with unit and visual regression tests, and distributed through an internal package registry. I would use semantic versioning, CI/CD automation, and governance processes to ensure multiple teams can adopt the library consistently without introducing breaking changes. This approach improves UI consistency, developer productivity, and long-term maintainability across all applications.

title: How Do You Handle API Rate Limits Gracefully?

content.overview: Handling API rate limits requires reducing unnecessary requests and implementing retry strategies for temporary failures.
content.approach: Use caching, debouncing, throttling, request deduplication, exponential backoff, and respect Retry-After headers.
content.interviewAnswer: To handle API rate limits gracefully, I first reduce unnecessary requests using debouncing, throttling, caching, and request deduplication. If a rate limit is hit, I handle HTTP 429 responses with exponential backoff and respect the Retry-After header. For high-volume applications, I may queue or batch requests and provide clear user feedback instead of exposing technical errors. In React applications, I commonly use TanStack Query for caching, retries, and request deduplication, which significantly reduces the likelihood of hitting rate limits.

title: How Would You Design a Frontend for 1M+ Users Daily?

content.overview: Applications serving millions of users require scalable rendering strategies, optimized performance, robust monitoring, and resilient architecture.
content.approach: Combine SSG, ISR, SSR, and CSR appropriately while optimizing caching, CDN delivery, monitoring, security, and deployment.
content.interviewAnswer: For a frontend serving 1M+ daily users, I would use a scalable architecture combining SSG, ISR, SSR, and CSR based on page requirements. I would optimize performance through code splitting, CDN delivery, caching, image optimization, and React Query. For large teams, I would adopt a feature-based or micro-frontend architecture with a shared component library. Additionally, I would implement monitoring, error tracking, security best practices, CI/CD automation, and Web Vitals observability to ensure reliability and performance at scale.

title: Tell Me About a Critical Production Bug

content.overview: Interviewers evaluate debugging skills, communication, ownership, and incident management through production bug discussions.
content.approach: Explain the problem, investigation, root cause, solution, outcome, and lessons learned.
content.interviewAnswer: In a previous e-commerce project, we encountered a critical production issue where users were being logged out after navigation and page refreshes. Since it affected authentication and checkout flows, it was treated as a high-priority incident. I reproduced the issue, analyzed browser storage, Redux state, network requests, and production logs. After investigation, I found that a deployment had introduced a change to the Redux Persist configuration key, which caused persisted authentication data to be lost after refreshes. I immediately reverted the change, deployed a hotfix, and verified that authentication persistence worked correctly. To prevent recurrence, I implemented state migration handling, added automated authentication regression tests, and updated our deployment checklist. The issue was resolved within about 30 minutes, user sessions stabilized, and checkout completion rates returned to normal.

title: Difference Between Reconciliation and Rendering

content.overview: Rendering and reconciliation are related but distinct phases in React's rendering pipeline.
content.approach: Rendering creates the new component tree, reconciliation compares it with the previous tree, and the commit phase updates the DOM.
content.interviewAnswer: Rendering creates the new React tree by executing components and generating a new Virtual DOM. Reconciliation compares the newly generated tree with the previous one using React's diffing algorithm to determine the minimal set of changes. Finally, during the commit phase, React applies those changes to the real DOM.

title: Why Are Hooks Not Allowed Inside Loops or Conditions?

content.overview: Hooks must always execute in the same order so React can correctly associate state and effects with component instances.
content.approach: Always call Hooks at the top level of the component and move conditional logic inside the Hook.
content.interviewAnswer: Hooks are not allowed inside loops, conditions, or nested functions because React relies on the order of Hook calls to associate state and effects with the correct component instance. During each render, React expects Hooks to be called in exactly the same sequence. If a Hook is skipped due to a condition or executed a different number of times in a loop, React can no longer correctly map state and effects, leading to bugs and inconsistent behavior. The correct approach is to always call Hooks at the top level of the component and place conditional logic inside the Hook itself.

title: Can useRef Cause Re-renders?

content.overview: Updating a useRef value does not trigger component re-rendering.
content.approach: Use refs for mutable values that persist across renders but do not affect the UI.
content.interviewAnswer: No, updating a useRef value does not trigger a re-render. A ref is a mutable object whose current property can be changed without notifying React. Unlike useState, React does not track changes to refs for rendering purposes. This makes useRef useful for storing DOM references, previous values, timers, or mutable data that should persist across renders without causing additional renders. The updated ref value becomes visible in the UI only when another state or prop update triggers a re-render.

title: useRef vs createRef

content.overview: Both createRef and useRef create references, but they are designed for different component types and lifecycles.
content.approach: Use createRef in class components and useRef in functional components because it persists across re-renders.
content.interviewAnswer: createRef and useRef are both used to create references in React, but they are intended for different component types. createRef is primarily used in class components and creates a new ref object every time it is called. In contrast, useRef is designed for functional components and returns the same ref object across re-renders. Because useRef persists between renders, it can also store mutable values such as timers, previous state values, or WebSocket instances without causing re-renders. In modern React applications, useRef is the preferred approach.

title: What Are Error Boundaries?

content.overview: Error Boundaries are React components that catch JavaScript errors in their child component tree and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the entire application.
content.approach: Implement Error Boundaries using class components with getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch. Place them around major feature areas and integrate them with monitoring tools.
content.interviewAnswer: Error Boundaries are React components that catch JavaScript errors in their child component tree during rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors. Instead of allowing the entire application to crash, they display a fallback UI and optionally log the error to monitoring services like Sentry. Error Boundaries are implemented using class components with getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch. They are useful for isolating failures in specific parts of an application, such as dashboards, checkout flows, or third-party widgets. However, they do not catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code, promise rejections, or server-side rendering. In production applications, I typically place Error Boundaries around major feature areas and integrate them with error monitoring tools for observability.
examples: Wrapping a checkout page with an Error Boundary

title: What Is List Virtualization?

content.overview: List virtualization renders only the visible portion of a large list, improving rendering performance and reducing memory usage.
content.approach: Use virtualization libraries such as react-window, react-virtualized, or TanStack Virtual to render only visible items.
content.interviewAnswer: List Virtualization, also known as windowing, is a performance optimization technique where only the items currently visible in the viewport are rendered instead of rendering the entire list. This significantly reduces the number of DOM nodes, improves memory usage, speeds up initial rendering, and provides smoother scrolling for large datasets. In React, libraries such as react-window, react-virtualized, or TanStack Virtual are commonly used to implement virtualization. For example, if a page contains 10,000 records, virtualization may render only 20–30 visible rows at a time and dynamically replace them as the user scrolls. I typically use virtualization in large tables, dashboards, chat applications, and product listings where rendering all items would negatively impact performance.

title: What Is Browser Reflow vs Repaint?

content.overview: Reflow recalculates layout, while repaint redraws visual changes without affecting layout.
content.approach: Minimize layout-triggering changes, batch DOM updates, and use GPU-accelerated properties for animations.
content.interviewAnswer: Reflow and repaint are browser rendering operations. Reflow, also called layout, occurs when the browser recalculates the size and position of elements due to changes such as width, height, margins, font size, or DOM structure. It is expensive because it may affect many elements on the page. Repaint occurs when an element's visual appearance changes, such as color or background color, without affecting layout. Repaint is generally less expensive because the browser only redraws pixels. Every reflow causes a repaint, but not every repaint causes a reflow. To improve performance, I try to minimize layout-triggering changes, batch DOM updates, use virtualization for large lists, and prefer GPU-accelerated properties like transform and opacity for animations.
examples: Using transform instead of top/left animations

title: What Is Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)?

content.overview: RBAC is an authorization model where users inherit permissions through assigned roles.
content.approach: Assign permissions to roles, protect routes and UI based on roles, and always validate authorization on the backend.
content.interviewAnswer: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is an authorization model where permissions are assigned to roles, and users inherit permissions through their assigned roles. Instead of managing permissions individually for each user, we define roles such as Admin, Manager, and Customer and associate permissions with those roles. In React applications, RBAC is commonly used to protect routes, conditionally render UI elements, and control feature access. However, frontend RBAC is mainly for user experience and should not be considered security. The backend must always validate permissions before executing sensitive operations. In large applications, I prefer a permission-based approach built on top of RBAC because it provides more flexibility and finer-grained control.

title: How Would You Handle API Retries?

content.overview: Retry only transient API failures using exponential backoff while avoiding retries for permanent client-side errors.
content.approach: Retry network failures, timeouts, rate limits, and 5xx errors with exponential backoff and jitter.
content.interviewAnswer: I retry only transient failures such as network issues, timeouts, rate limits, and 5xx server errors. I avoid retrying client-side errors like 400 or 401 because retries won't fix them. My preferred approach is exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum retry count, and respecting Retry-After headers when available. In React applications, I often use TanStack Query for built-in retry handling and caching. I also ensure users receive clear feedback and avoid retrying non-idempotent operations like order creation unless idempotency mechanisms are in place.

title: How Would You Secure Authentication?

content.overview: Secure authentication requires layered security, secure token storage, and backend authorization validation.
content.approach: Use HTTPS, short-lived access tokens, HttpOnly cookies, refresh token rotation, RBAC, and backend validation.
content.interviewAnswer: To secure authentication, I use HTTPS, short-lived access tokens, refresh token rotation, and HttpOnly secure cookies instead of localStorage whenever possible. I protect against XSS through sanitization and Content Security Policies, and against CSRF using SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens. I implement RBAC for authorization, automatic token refresh using interceptors, secure logout, session expiration, rate limiting, and backend-side permission checks. Most importantly, I treat the frontend as untrusted and ensure all authentication and authorization decisions are validated on the server.

title: Monolith vs Micro Frontend

content.overview: Monolithic frontends are simpler to manage, while micro frontends enable independent team ownership and deployments.
content.approach: Start with a well-structured monolith and adopt micro frontends only when organizational scale requires them.
content.interviewAnswer: A monolithic frontend is a single application where all features are developed, built, and deployed together. It is simpler to develop, test, and maintain initially, making it a good choice for small to medium-sized teams and applications. A micro frontend architecture splits the frontend into independently developed and deployed applications, each owned by a specific team or domain. This improves scalability, team autonomy, and deployment flexibility but introduces additional complexity around routing, communication, shared dependencies, and testing. For most projects, I would start with a well-structured monolith using a feature-based architecture. I would only move to micro frontends when organizational scale, team size, or deployment requirements justify the added complexity.
examples: E-commerce split into authentication, catalog, and checkout

title: How Would You Debug Production Performance Issues?

content.overview: Production performance issues should be investigated using monitoring tools, profiling, and data-driven optimization.
content.approach: Identify the bottleneck, reproduce the issue, profile it, optimize, and verify improvements using real user metrics.
content.interviewAnswer: I debug production performance issues using a data-driven approach. I start with monitoring tools like Sentry or Datadog to identify affected pages and performance metrics. Then I reproduce the issue and use Chrome DevTools, Lighthouse, and the React Profiler to determine whether the bottleneck is rendering, network requests, memory leaks, bundle size, or backend latency. After identifying the root cause, I apply targeted optimizations such as memoization, virtualization, caching, code splitting, or API improvements, and then verify the results using Web Vitals and real user monitoring before deployment.

title: What Is Module Federation?

content.overview: Module Federation is a Webpack 5 feature that enables applications to share modules at runtime.
content.approach: Expose and consume remote modules dynamically to enable independently deployed micro frontends.
content.interviewAnswer: Module Federation is a Webpack 5 feature that enables applications to share and consume modules from other applications at runtime. It is commonly used in micro frontend architectures, where different teams own and deploy independent frontend applications. A host application dynamically loads components or modules exposed by remote applications without requiring a rebuild. The main benefits are independent deployments, team autonomy, code sharing, and reduced duplication of shared dependencies like React. However, Module Federation introduces additional complexity around routing, dependency management, version compatibility, and testing, so I use it only when organizational scale justifies it.

title: How Does React Measure Component Changes?

content.overview: React measures component changes using the Virtual DOM and reconciliation to minimize expensive DOM updates.
content.approach: Generate a new Virtual DOM tree, compare it with the previous tree, and update only the changed parts of the real DOM.
content.interviewAnswer: React measures component changes using the Virtual DOM and a process called reconciliation. When state or props change, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and compares it with the previous one using a diffing algorithm. Based on this comparison, React determines the minimal set of changes required and updates only those parts of the real DOM. React uses heuristics such as comparing element types and keys to make diffing efficient. Components re-render when state changes, props change, or parent components re-render. React Fiber further improves this process by prioritizing updates and allowing rendering work to be paused and resumed. This approach minimizes expensive DOM operations and helps React deliver high performance.
examples: Updating a product list after state changes

title: How Do You Measure React Performance?

content.overview: React performance is measured using profiling tools, browser performance analysis, Web Vitals, and production monitoring.
content.approach: Profile rendering, analyze browser performance, monitor Web Vitals, optimize bottlenecks, and validate improvements using before-and-after metrics.
content.interviewAnswer: In production React applications, I usually start with React DevTools Profiler to identify expensive renders and unnecessary re-renders. Then I use Chrome DevTools Performance and Network tabs to analyze JavaScript execution, API latency, and rendering costs. I also monitor Web Vitals such as LCP, INP, and CLS using Lighthouse and production monitoring tools like Sentry. Based on the findings, I optimize using React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, virtualization, code splitting, caching with TanStack Query, and bundle-size reduction. Finally, I compare performance metrics before and after the optimization to validate the improvement.

title: What is ForwardRef in React?

content.overview: forwardRef allows a parent component to pass a ref through a child component to its underlying DOM element or instance.
content.approach: Wrap functional components with forwardRef and optionally combine it with useImperativeHandle to expose controlled APIs.
content.interviewAnswer: forwardRef is a React API used to forward a ref from a parent component to a child component's DOM element or instance. By default, refs cannot be attached to function components because they do not expose their internal DOM nodes. Using forwardRef, we can pass the ref through the component and attach it to a specific DOM element. It is commonly used in reusable component libraries, form inputs, modals, and when integrating with third-party DOM-based libraries. It is often combined with useImperativeHandle to expose only selected methods rather than the entire DOM element.

title: Explain Compound Component Pattern

content.overview: The Compound Component Pattern enables related components to share state implicitly through a parent component, creating flexible and declarative APIs.
content.approach: Manage shared state in the parent using Context API and allow child components to consume it without prop drilling.
content.interviewAnswer: The Compound Component Pattern is a React pattern where a parent component manages shared state and child components consume that state implicitly, usually through Context API. Instead of passing many configuration props, consumers compose related components together using JSX. This creates a clean, flexible, and declarative API. Common examples include Tabs, Accordions, Modals, Dropdowns, and Form Fields. The main advantages are avoiding prop drilling, improving reusability, encapsulating state, and creating APIs similar to native HTML elements. In modern React applications, compound components are typically implemented using Context API rather than cloneElement.

title: What are Children Props?

content.overview: The children prop represents content passed between a component's opening and closing tags.
content.approach: Render children inside reusable wrapper components and use React.Children utilities when child manipulation is required.
content.interviewAnswer: The children prop is a special React prop that represents the content passed between a component's opening and closing tags. It allows components to be highly reusable and composable by rendering dynamic content inside them. Common examples include Layouts, Cards, Modals, and Buttons. React also provides the React.Children API for counting, mapping, and transforming child elements. In TypeScript, children is typically typed as ReactNode.

title: What is Middleware and Why is it Used?

content.overview: Middleware is an intermediate processing layer that intercepts requests or actions before they reach the final handler.
content.approach: Use middleware to implement reusable cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, logging, validation, and error handling.
content.interviewAnswer: Middleware is a processing layer that intercepts requests or actions before they reach the final handler, enabling reusable logic such as authentication, logging, validation, and error handling. By separating these concerns from business logic, middleware improves code maintainability, consistency, and scalability.

title: Explain the Architecture of Your Current Project (React + TypeScript)

content.overview: A scalable React + TypeScript project typically follows a feature-based modular architecture with centralized services and reusable components.
content.approach: Organize code by business domains, separate presentation from business logic, centralize API communication, and optimize performance with modern React techniques.
content.interviewAnswer: In my current React + TypeScript project, we follow a feature-based modular architecture. The application is divided into business domains such as authentication, products, orders, and customer management. We use TypeScript for type safety, Redux Toolkit for global state management, and custom hooks to separate business logic from presentation components. API communication is centralized through service layers using Axios with interceptors for authentication and error handling. Shared UI components are maintained in a reusable design system, while routing is handled through protected routes and role-based access control. For performance, we implement lazy loading, code splitting, memoization, and virtualization where required. The project is supported by automated testing, CI/CD pipelines, accessibility standards, and multiple deployment environments, ensuring scalability and maintainability for enterprise-level applications.

title: Why Did You Choose Feature-Based Architecture Instead of Layer-Based Architecture?

content.overview: Feature-based architecture organizes code by business domains, improving scalability and reducing coupling.
content.approach: Group components, hooks, services, tests, and types by feature so teams can work independently.
content.interviewAnswer: Feature-based architecture scales better in large teams because each feature owns its components, hooks, services, types, and tests. This reduces coupling, improves maintainability, and allows teams to work independently without affecting unrelated modules. Compared to layer-based architecture, it keeps related code together, making features easier to develop, test, and evolve.

title: How Would You Implement Infinite Scrolling in React?

content.overview: Infinite scrolling loads additional data automatically as the user reaches the end of the visible content.
content.approach: Use the Intersection Observer API with paginated APIs, React Query's useInfiniteQuery, and virtualization for large datasets.
content.interviewAnswer: In React, I implement infinite scrolling using the Intersection Observer API. I place a sentinel element at the bottom of the list and observe it. When it enters the viewport, I fetch the next page and append the results to the existing state. This approach is more efficient than scroll event listeners because it avoids continuous event execution. For production applications, I combine it with React Query's useInfiniteQuery for pagination and caching, prevent duplicate requests with loading flags, handle end-of-list scenarios using a hasMore flag, and use virtualization libraries like react-window when rendering thousands of records to maintain smooth performance.

title: How Would You Build Search with Live Filtering?

content.overview: Live search filters results as users type while maintaining responsiveness and minimizing unnecessary work.
content.approach: Use client-side filtering for small datasets, server-side searching for large datasets, debounce API calls, and cache responses.
content.interviewAnswer: To build live search in React, I would maintain the search term in state and trigger filtering as the user types. For small datasets, I use client-side filtering with Array.filter() and optimize expensive computations using useMemo. For large datasets, I perform server-side searching and debounce the input using a custom hook or lodash debounce to avoid excessive API calls. I also handle race conditions using AbortController, cache responses with React Query, and use useDeferredValue or list virtualization when dealing with large result sets. This ensures the search remains responsive, scalable, and performant even with thousands of records.

title: How Would You Design Dynamic Forms?

content.overview: Dynamic forms use schema-driven configuration to generate fields instead of hardcoding form structures.
content.approach: Build a form renderer using reusable field components, React Hook Form, schema definitions, and backend-driven validation.
content.interviewAnswer: In enterprise applications, I design dynamic forms using a schema-driven architecture where field definitions come from configuration or APIs rather than being hardcoded. I create a form renderer that maps field types to reusable components using a component factory pattern. For state management and validation, I typically use React Hook Form because it minimizes re-renders and performs well with large forms. I support conditional rendering, dependent fields, dynamic field arrays, and backend-driven validation rules. This approach makes forms highly reusable, scalable, and maintainable, especially in multi-tenant applications where form structures change frequently without requiring frontend deployments.

title: How to Improve SEO in React Application?

content.overview: Improving SEO in React involves choosing the right rendering strategy, optimizing metadata, performance, accessibility, and search engine discoverability.
content.approach: Use SSR or SSG for SEO-critical pages, optimize metadata, generate sitemaps, improve Core Web Vitals, and follow accessibility best practices.
content.interviewAnswer: To improve SEO in a React application, I first determine the rendering strategy. For content-heavy pages, I prefer SSR or SSG using Next.js because search engines can immediately crawl the generated HTML. I ensure every page has dynamic meta tags using React Helmet or Next.js Head, implement structured data with Schema.org, generate sitemap.xml and robots.txt files, and use canonical URLs to prevent duplicate content issues. I also optimize performance through code splitting, lazy loading, image optimization, and caching because Core Web Vitals impact search rankings. Additionally, I follow accessibility best practices with semantic HTML and proper alt attributes, which improve both usability and SEO.

title: When Should You NOT Use Redux?

content.overview: Redux should be avoided when application state is simple or can be managed effectively using React's built-in state management solutions.
content.approach: Keep state as close as possible to where it is used and introduce Redux only when shared client-side state becomes sufficiently complex.
content.interviewAnswer: I avoid Redux when the application has simple state requirements, such as local UI state, parent-child communication, or lightweight global state like themes and authentication context. For API data, I prefer React Query because it provides caching, synchronization, retries, and loading states out of the box. Redux becomes valuable when there is complex shared client-side state, business workflows, or large-scale applications where state is accessed and modified across many unrelated components. My principle is to keep the state as close as possible to where it's used and introduce Redux only when the complexity justifies the additional architecture.

title: What Are Selectors and Why Are They Important?

content.overview: Selectors extract or derive data from the Redux store while improving maintainability, performance, and reusability.
content.approach: Create reusable selectors and memoize expensive derived computations using createSelector.
content.interviewAnswer: Selectors are functions that extract or derive data from the Redux store. They help decouple components from the store structure, making the codebase easier to maintain and refactor. Beyond simple data access, selectors can compute derived values such as filtered lists, totals, or aggregated metrics. For expensive computations, I use memoized selectors with createSelector from Redux Toolkit or Reselect, which cache results and recompute only when relevant state changes. This improves performance, promotes reusability, simplifies testing, and keeps Redux state normalized by avoiding storage of derived data.

title: Explain Redux Performance Optimization

content.overview: Redux performance optimization focuses on minimizing unnecessary re-renders, efficient state updates, and optimized data selection.
content.approach: Use memoized selectors, normalized state, optimized subscriptions, RTK Query, and component memoization.
content.interviewAnswer: Redux performance optimization is primarily about reducing unnecessary React re-renders and expensive computations. I use memoized selectors with createSelector to cache derived data, normalize state using createEntityAdapter for efficient updates, and ensure components subscribe only to the specific state they need through useSelector. I avoid storing local UI state in Redux and use React.memo to prevent unnecessary child renders. For API data, I prefer RTK Query because it provides caching and request deduplication out of the box. In large applications, I split components, lazy-load modules, and keep the Redux store normalized so updates remain efficient and scalable.

title: Why Redux Toolkit over Traditional Redux?

content.overview: Redux Toolkit is the official Redux solution that simplifies Redux development while following best practices.
content.approach: Use Redux Toolkit to reduce boilerplate, simplify immutable updates, configure the store, and handle asynchronous operations.
content.interviewAnswer: Redux Toolkit eliminates boilerplate, provides Immer for immutable updates, includes Redux DevTools configuration, async handling through createAsyncThunk, normalized state management, and RTK Query for API caching. It is now the official recommended way to write Redux applications and significantly improves maintainability in large-scale React applications.

title: What Happens Internally When You Call setState?

content.overview: Calling setState schedules an update through React Fiber instead of immediately updating the component state.
content.approach: React queues the update, schedules rendering, performs reconciliation, batches updates, and commits only the necessary DOM changes.
content.interviewAnswer: When setState is called, React creates an update object and places it into the Fiber update queue rather than updating state immediately. The scheduler assigns a priority to the update and schedules a render. During the render phase, React builds a new Virtual DOM tree and performs reconciliation by comparing it with the previous tree. It calculates the minimal set of changes required and then applies those changes to the real DOM during the commit phase. React batches multiple state updates together for performance, and in React 18 automatic batching works across events, promises, and timeouts. This architecture allows React to efficiently update the UI while supporting concurrent rendering and prioritized work.

title: How Does React Decide What to Re-render?

content.overview: React re-renders components whenever the data they depend on changes.
content.approach: Understand the triggers for rendering and optimize unnecessary renders using memoization techniques.
content.interviewAnswer: React decides to re-render a component when its state changes, its props change, the context it consumes changes, or its parent component re-renders. During rendering, React performs reconciliation to determine whether the resulting DOM output has changed before committing updates.

title: How Do React Server Components Change Data Fetching?

content.overview: React Server Components move initial data fetching from the browser to the server, reducing client-side JavaScript and improving performance.
content.approach: Fetch data directly inside Server Components and use Client Components only for interactive functionality.
content.interviewAnswer: React Server Components shift data fetching from the browser to the server. Instead of fetching data in useEffect after the page loads, a Server Component can directly execute async data fetching or database queries before rendering. This eliminates many client-side API requests, reduces JavaScript bundle size, improves initial page load performance, and keeps sensitive credentials on the server. In frameworks like Next.js App Router, Server Components are the default for data-heavy pages, while Client Components are used only for interactive features such as forms, state management, and event handling. In practice, I use Server Components for initial data loading and React Query or client-side state management for dynamic user interactions after hydration.

title: How Would You Scale This Component to Handle 1 Million Users?

content.overview: Scaling for millions of users requires frontend optimization, efficient caching, CDN delivery, scalable infrastructure, and continuous monitoring.
content.approach: Optimize rendering, cache data, scale backend services, and monitor application performance continuously.
content.interviewAnswer: To scale for 1M users, I would optimize rendering with virtualization and memoization, cache API responses using React Query and Redis, use CDN delivery, horizontally scale backend services, and continuously monitor performance through observability tools. This combination ensures responsive user interfaces, efficient resource utilization, and reliable application performance under heavy traffic.

title: What Is The Most Challenging Task You Handled In Your Project?

content.overview: Interviewers use this question to evaluate problem-solving ability, technical depth, ownership, and measurable business impact.
content.approach: Describe the challenge, explain your investigation and solution, and highlight measurable improvements.
content.interviewAnswer: The most challenging task I handled was improving application performance for a large e-commerce platform where page load times exceeded 8 seconds. By implementing code splitting, lazy loading, memoization, API caching, image optimization, and bundle analysis, I reduced load time to under 3 seconds and improved Core Web Vitals significantly, resulting in better user experience and conversion rates.

title: Have You Used Redux Toolkit Or TanStack Query?

content.overview: Redux Toolkit and TanStack Query solve different problems. Redux Toolkit manages client-side state, while TanStack Query manages server state and API synchronization.
content.approach: Use Redux Toolkit for global client state such as authentication, UI preferences, and business workflows. Use TanStack Query for API requests, caching, synchronization, retries, and background refetching.
content.interviewAnswer: Yes, I have used both. Redux Toolkit is ideal for client-side global state, whereas TanStack Query is designed for server state management, caching, synchronization, and API handling. I typically use Redux Toolkit for application state like authentication, user preferences, and UI state, while using TanStack Query for API data because it provides caching, request deduplication, background refetching, retries, and stale data management out of the box.
whenToUse: Redux Toolkit for global application state

title: A Component Is Re-rendering Too Many Times. How Would You Debug It?

content.overview: Debug excessive re-renders by profiling the application, identifying the root cause, and applying targeted optimizations.
content.approach: Use React DevTools Profiler, inspect state updates, prop changes, context updates, and parent renders before applying memoization techniques.
content.interviewAnswer: I would first use React DevTools Profiler to identify which component is re-rendering frequently and why. Then I would check for unnecessary state updates, parent component re-renders, new object or function references being passed as props, and context updates affecting child components. Based on the findings, I would use React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, or split components to reduce rendering. I always optimize only after measuring the actual bottleneck.

title: Your Application Has a Large Form With Complex Validation. How Would You Implement It?

content.overview: Large forms should be built with scalable architecture, reusable components, and efficient validation.
content.approach: Use React Hook Form with schema validation, reusable field components, and optimized rendering.
content.interviewAnswer: For large forms, I typically use React Hook Form because it minimizes re-renders and provides excellent performance. My approach is to define reusable form components, use schema-based validation with Yup or Zod, implement field-level validation, carefully handle dependent fields, save draft data when necessary, and display clear validation messages. This keeps forms scalable, maintainable, and performant.

title: Users Report Data Inconsistency Across Screens. How Would You Investigate?

content.overview: Data inconsistency can originate from frontend state, API responses, caching, or backend synchronization.
content.approach: Verify API responses, inspect state management, analyze caching behavior, and implement proper cache invalidation if necessary.
content.interviewAnswer: First, I would identify whether the issue originates from frontend state management, API responses, or backend synchronization. I would inspect API payloads, Redux or Context state, caching mechanisms, and component lifecycle behavior. If stale data is the issue, I would implement proper cache invalidation, refetch strategies, or centralized state management to ensure consistency across screens.

title: A New Feature Is Requested With a Very Tight Deadline. What Is Your Approach?

content.overview: Deliver value quickly by prioritizing the MVP while maintaining quality and minimizing technical debt.
content.approach: Clarify requirements, define the MVP, prioritize work, reuse existing components, and deliver incrementally.
content.interviewAnswer: I first clarify requirements and identify the Minimum Viable Product (MVP). Then I break the feature into smaller tasks, prioritize critical functionality, reuse existing components whenever possible, deliver incrementally, and maintain testing for critical flows. Even under pressure, I avoid shortcuts that create long-term technical debt.

title: How Do You Handle Conflicting Requirements From Stakeholders?

content.overview: Conflicting requirements should be resolved through collaboration, technical analysis, and business prioritization.
content.approach: Understand business goals, document trade-offs, and help stakeholders make informed decisions.
content.interviewAnswer: I facilitate discussions with stakeholders and product owners to understand the business goals behind each requirement. I document the impact, risks, development effort, and user experience implications. Then I provide technical recommendations and help stakeholders make informed decisions based on business priorities.

title: How Do You Approach Code Reviews?

content.overview: Code reviews improve code quality, maintainability, knowledge sharing, and team collaboration.
content.approach: Review code objectively, provide constructive feedback, and focus on long-term maintainability.
content.interviewAnswer: I focus on readability, maintainability, performance, security, and test coverage. I avoid personal opinions and provide constructive feedback with explanations. My goal is knowledge sharing and improving overall code quality rather than simply finding mistakes.

title: How Do You Ensure React Application Scalability?

content.overview: Scalable React applications require modular architecture, reusable components, optimized performance, and development standards.
content.approach: Adopt feature-based architecture, reusable components, code splitting, centralized state, testing, and coding standards.
content.interviewAnswer: I focus on a feature-based folder structure, reusable components, TypeScript adoption, centralized state management, code splitting, lazy loading, proper API abstraction, and automated testing. I also enforce coding standards through ESLint, Prettier, and pull request reviews to maintain consistency and scalability as the application grows.

title: How Would You Handle Real-Time Updates in React?

content.overview: Real-time applications require efficient communication mechanisms and careful state management.
content.approach: Choose WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, or polling based on application requirements while efficiently updating state.
content.interviewAnswer: For real-time features like notifications, chat, or dashboards, I typically use WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE), or polling when real-time communication is not mandatory. I manage connections carefully, handle reconnections, clean up subscriptions, and update state efficiently to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

title: A Page Takes 10 Seconds to Load. What Would You Do?

content.overview: Diagnose slow page loads by analyzing network activity, rendering performance, bundle size, and backend response times.
content.approach: Measure first, identify bottlenecks, optimize incrementally, and validate improvements using performance tools.
content.interviewAnswer: I would analyze network requests, bundle size, API performance, and rendering performance. Common optimizations include code splitting, lazy loading, image optimization, API pagination, caching, and virtualized lists. I use Lighthouse and React Profiler to validate improvements and compare performance metrics before and after optimization.

title: How Do You Handle Authentication and Authorization in React?

content.overview: Authentication verifies user identity, while authorization determines what resources or actions the authenticated user can access.
content.approach: Implement secure authentication using JWT or OAuth, protect routes, enforce role-based access, and always validate permissions on the backend.
content.interviewAnswer: Authentication verifies the user, while authorization determines access rights. My approach is to use JWT or OAuth-based authentication, implement secure token handling, protect routes, apply Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), and always validate permissions on the backend. I never rely solely on frontend authorization because security must always be enforced on the server side.

title: Your Redux Store Is Becoming Very Large. What Would You Do?

content.overview: A large Redux store should be simplified by storing only shared business state and keeping other state closer to where it is used.
content.approach: Separate UI state, server state, and business state while organizing Redux using feature slices and normalized data.
content.interviewAnswer: I avoid putting everything into Redux. I keep UI state local, server state in React Query or TanStack Query, and global business state in Redux. I also split Redux slices by feature and normalize data structures to keep the store manageable, scalable, and performant.

title: How Would You Migrate a JavaScript React Application to TypeScript?

content.overview: Migrating incrementally minimizes risk while improving type safety and maintainability.
content.approach: Configure TypeScript, migrate files gradually, introduce interfaces, resolve type errors progressively, and enforce strict typing.
content.interviewAnswer: I would migrate gradually instead of rewriting everything. First, I configure TypeScript and rename files incrementally. I start with reusable components, then add interfaces and types while fixing type errors progressively. Finally, I enable stricter compiler settings and enforce strict typing through CI/CD. This minimizes risk while steadily improving code quality.

title: How Do You Ensure Accessibility in React Applications?

content.overview: Accessibility ensures applications are usable by people with diverse abilities while improving overall user experience.
content.approach: Follow WCAG guidelines, use semantic HTML, support keyboard navigation, test with assistive technologies, and automate accessibility checks.
content.interviewAnswer: I follow WCAG guidelines by using semantic HTML, supporting keyboard navigation, providing ARIA attributes, maintaining sufficient color contrast, and testing with screen readers. I also use automated accessibility tools such as axe and Lighthouse during development to identify accessibility issues early.

title: A Third-Party Library Is Causing Performance Issues. What Would You Do?

content.overview: Performance issues caused by third-party libraries should be validated before deciding whether to optimize, replace, or remove them.
content.approach: Profile the application, evaluate optimization opportunities, and replace the library only if necessary.
content.interviewAnswer: I first profile the application to verify the library is the root cause. Then I evaluate upgrading the library, tree-shaking opportunities, dynamic imports, and lightweight alternatives. If necessary, I replace the library with a custom implementation that better fits the project's requirements while maintaining functionality and improving performance.

title: Describe a Challenging React Problem You Solved

content.overview: Interviewers evaluate problem-solving ability through real production challenges and measurable outcomes.
content.approach: Describe the problem, investigation, implementation, and measurable business impact.
content.interviewAnswer: In one project, a dashboard with thousands of records became slow and unresponsive. I investigated using React Profiler and identified excessive rendering and large DOM updates. I implemented list virtualization, memoization, API pagination, lazy loading, and optimized Redux selectors. As a result, page load time dropped significantly, rendering became much faster, and user interactions became noticeably smoother.

title: What Happens After Browser Downloads React Bundle?

content.overview: After downloading the React bundle, the browser executes JavaScript, React renders the application, and the browser paints the UI.
content.approach: Understand the complete lifecycle from JavaScript execution to browser rendering.
content.interviewAnswer: After the browser downloads the React bundle, it parses and executes the JavaScript. React creates the component tree, builds the Virtual DOM, performs reconciliation through the Fiber architecture, and calculates the minimum DOM updates. During the commit phase, those changes are applied to the real DOM. Finally, the browser performs layout, paint, and compositing to display the user interface on the screen.

title: What Is a CI Pipeline?

content.overview: A CI pipeline automates build validation to ensure code quality and deployment readiness after every code change.
content.approach: Automate dependency installation, linting, testing, building, and artifact generation whenever code is committed.
content.interviewAnswer: A CI Pipeline is an automated workflow that runs whenever code is pushed to a repository. It typically installs dependencies, performs linting, executes automated tests, builds the application, and generates deployment artifacts. The primary purpose is to catch issues early, maintain code quality, and ensure that the application remains deployable. In React projects, I commonly configure CI pipelines to run ESLint, unit tests using Jest and React Testing Library, build the production bundle, and publish artifacts through Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions before deployment.

title: What Is a Build Artifact in CI/CD?

content.overview: A build artifact is the deployable output produced during the build stage of a CI pipeline.
content.approach: Generate production-ready assets once, store them securely, and deploy the same artifact across environments.
content.interviewAnswer: A build artifact is the deployable output generated by the build stage of a CI pipeline. For a React application, it is typically the build or dist folder containing optimized HTML, CSS, and JavaScript bundles. Artifacts are stored in an artifact repository and promoted through QA, staging, and production environments. Using artifacts ensures deployment consistency, enables versioning and rollback, and avoids rebuilding the application for each environment.

title: Deployment Strategies

content.overview: Deployment strategies reduce release risk while ensuring high availability and smooth software rollouts.
content.approach: Choose the deployment strategy based on business risk, infrastructure, and rollback requirements.
content.interviewAnswer: Deployment strategies are approaches used to release new software versions while minimizing downtime and risk. Common strategies include Rolling Deployment, where instances are updated gradually; Blue-Green Deployment, where traffic is switched between two identical environments; Canary Deployment, where a small percentage of users receive the new version first; and Feature Flags, which allow features to be enabled or disabled without redeployment. In enterprise React applications, Canary releases and Feature Flags are commonly used because they reduce risk, allow gradual rollouts, and provide quick rollback options.

title: How Do You Secure CI/CD Pipelines?

content.overview: Securing CI/CD pipelines requires protecting secrets, controlling access, validating dependencies, and ensuring deployment integrity.
content.approach: Secure credentials, enforce least privilege, automate security scanning, protect build artifacts, and audit deployments.
content.interviewAnswer: To secure CI/CD pipelines, I focus on multiple layers of protection. Secrets are stored in secure vaults rather than source control, and pipeline identities follow the principle of least privilege. Branch protection rules enforce pull request reviews and automated quality checks before merges. The pipeline includes static code analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, and artifact scanning before deployment. Build artifacts are immutable and digitally signed to prevent tampering. Production deployments require approval gates, and all actions are audited and monitored. For frontend applications, I also ensure sensitive values are never embedded in the client bundle and that dependency security checks run as part of every build.

title: What is Pipeline as Code?

content.overview: Pipeline as Code stores CI/CD pipeline definitions as version-controlled code, enabling consistency, automation, and collaboration.
content.approach: Define CI/CD workflows using YAML, store them in Git, review changes through pull requests, and version pipeline configurations alongside application code.
content.interviewAnswer: In enterprise projects, we use Pipeline as Code to ensure CI/CD processes are treated like application code. Pipeline definitions are stored in Git repositories and reviewed through pull requests. This allows us to version pipeline changes, enforce quality checks, standardize deployments across multiple applications, and easily roll back changes if needed. In React projects, our Azure DevOps YAML pipelines typically handle dependency installation, linting, testing, artifact generation, security scans, and deployment promotion through various environments, all managed through source-controlled configuration files.

title: Monorepo Impact on CI/CD

content.overview: Monorepos simplify code sharing and standardize CI/CD but require optimized pipelines to avoid unnecessary builds.
content.approach: Use path-based triggers, affected builds, dependency graphs, caching, and parallel execution to reduce build time.
content.interviewAnswer: A monorepo can simplify code sharing, dependency management, and CI/CD standardization because multiple applications and libraries live in a single repository. However, it can also increase build times and pipeline complexity if every change triggers a full build. To address this, modern CI/CD pipelines use path-based triggers, dependency graph analysis, affected builds, caching, and parallel execution. In React monorepos using Nx or Turborepo, we typically run only the affected builds and tests, which significantly reduces pipeline execution time and resource consumption.

title: How Do You Handle Environment Variables?

content.overview: Environment variables separate configuration from application code while protecting sensitive information.
content.approach: Expose only non-sensitive frontend variables, manage secrets securely, and inject environment-specific values during deployment.
content.interviewAnswer: I treat configuration separately from code using environment variables and secret management solutions. For frontend applications, I only expose non-sensitive values such as API URLs and feature flags. Secrets remain on the backend and are managed through Azure Key Vault or equivalent secret stores. In CI/CD, environment-specific variables are injected during deployment, allowing the same build artifact to be promoted across QA, staging, and production while using different configurations. This improves security, consistency, and deployment reliability.

title: What is a Multi-Branch Pipeline?

content.overview: A multi-branch pipeline automatically validates code changes independently for every branch.
content.approach: Configure CI to execute builds, tests, linting, and security checks for feature, release, and main branches.
content.interviewAnswer: In enterprise projects, we use multi-branch pipelines to ensure every feature, release, and main branch is automatically validated through the CI process. Each branch runs linting, unit tests, security scans, and build steps independently. Pull request policies require successful pipeline execution before merging. This approach improves development velocity, reduces integration issues, and ensures only verified code progresses through the release pipeline.

title: What are Microservices?

content.overview: Microservices is an architectural style where an application is divided into independently deployable services with specific business responsibilities.
content.approach: Split the application into domain-focused services that communicate through APIs or messaging systems.
content.interviewAnswer: Microservices is an architectural style where an application is split into multiple independent services. Each service has its own business responsibility, can be deployed independently, ideally owns its own database, and communicates through APIs or messaging systems. For example, an e-commerce application may have separate User, Product, Order, Payment, and Notification services. The main benefits include independent deployment, better scalability, fault isolation, and technology flexibility. However, microservices also introduce challenges such as distributed system complexity, network latency, monitoring, and debugging.

title: Offline Functionality & Synchronization

content.overview: Offline-first applications allow users to continue working without network connectivity and synchronize changes when connectivity is restored.
content.approach: Cache assets, store offline data locally, queue user actions, and synchronize them safely after reconnection.
content.interviewAnswer: Offline functionality allows users to continue using the application without internet connectivity. In React applications, I typically use Service Workers for caching assets, IndexedDB for storing large offline data, and localStorage for smaller preferences. User actions performed offline are stored in a local queue and marked as pending. When connectivity is restored, a synchronization process sends the pending changes to the server. For conflict resolution, I prefer versioning or merge strategies instead of Last Write Wins to prevent data loss. In production applications, I've used React Query with persisted caches and Service Workers to provide an offline-first experience with background synchronization.

title: Creating and Using Custom Hooks

content.overview: Custom Hooks encapsulate reusable stateful logic so it can be shared across multiple components.
content.approach: Extract repeated logic into reusable hooks while following the Rules of Hooks.
content.interviewAnswer: Custom Hooks allow reusable stateful logic to be shared across multiple components without duplicating code. A custom hook is simply a JavaScript function whose name starts with 'use' and that can call other React Hooks. They are commonly used for data fetching, form handling, authentication, event listeners, and reusable business logic. Custom Hooks improve code organization, readability, and maintainability while keeping components focused on rendering.

title: What are HOCs (Higher-Order Components)?

content.overview: A Higher-Order Component is a function that accepts a component and returns an enhanced component with additional behavior.
content.approach: Wrap components to reuse cross-cutting concerns while avoiding duplication.
content.interviewAnswer: A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a function that takes a component as input and returns a new enhanced component. HOCs are commonly used to add reusable functionality such as authentication, authorization, logging, analytics, or feature flags without modifying the original component. Although Hooks are preferred in modern React, HOCs are still common in legacy applications and some third-party libraries.

title: How Would You Create a Real-Time Notification System in React?

content.overview: A scalable notification system requires reliable real-time communication, persistent storage, and efficient state management.
content.approach: Use WebSockets, persistent storage, scalable messaging infrastructure, and resilient client-side connection management.
content.interviewAnswer: For a production-grade notification system, I'd use Socket.IO or WebSockets for real-time delivery, persist notifications in a database, maintain unread counts, and manage state through Redux Toolkit or Context API. To scale across multiple servers, I'd introduce Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka between services and WebSocket gateways. I would also implement reconnection logic, browser notifications, notification history, user-specific channels, and role-based targeting. This architecture supports real-time updates while remaining scalable and fault-tolerant.

title: Function Component vs Class Component

content.overview: Function Components are the modern React standard, while Class Components are primarily maintained for legacy code and Error Boundaries.
content.approach: Prefer Function Components with Hooks for new development while understanding Class Components for maintaining existing applications.
content.interviewAnswer: Class Components are the older way of creating React components. They use this.state for state management, lifecycle methods like componentDidMount, and require the this keyword. Function Components are the modern approach. They use React Hooks such as useState and useEffect to manage state and side effects, making the code simpler, cleaner, and easier to maintain. Function Components are preferred because they require less boilerplate, avoid this binding issues, enable reusable logic through Hooks, and provide better readability and maintainability. Today, Function Components are the standard choice, while Class Components are mainly used in legacy applications and for Error Boundaries.

title: What is TypeScript, and why would you choose it over JavaScript?

content.overview: TypeScript is a statically typed superset of JavaScript developed by Microsoft. It adds optional static typing, interfaces, generics, decorators (experimental), enums, and advanced type features while compiling to plain JavaScript.
approach: Explain that TypeScript is compiled into JavaScript.
Highlight static typing and compile-time error detection.
Discuss improved IDE support and maintainability.
content.interviewAnswer: TypeScript extends JavaScript by introducing static typing and advanced language features while remaining fully compatible with JavaScript. During development, TypeScript performs type checking at compile time, helping developers catch errors before runtime. Since it compiles into standard JavaScript, it works in all browsers and Node.js environments. In enterprise applications with large teams and codebases, TypeScript significantly improves code quality, maintainability, scalability, refactoring safety, and developer productivity through features like IntelliSense, generics, interfaces, and strict type checking.
bestPractices: Prefer explicit typing for public APIs.
followUpQuestions: How does TypeScript compile to JavaScript?
Can JavaScript files be used inside a TypeScript project?

title: How does TypeScript differ from JavaScript?

content.overview: JavaScript is dynamically typed, whereas TypeScript adds optional static typing and compile-time analysis.
content.interviewAnswer: JavaScript determines types at runtime, making it flexible but prone to runtime errors. TypeScript introduces static type checking during compilation, allowing developers to catch mistakes early. It also provides interfaces, enums, generics, utility types, access modifiers, and advanced type inference. While JavaScript focuses on execution, TypeScript focuses on improving development experience and maintainability without changing runtime behavior.
followUpQuestions: Is every JavaScript program valid TypeScript?

title: What is Type Inference in TypeScript?

content.overview: Type inference allows TypeScript to automatically determine variable and expression types without explicit annotations.
content.interviewAnswer: Type inference is one of TypeScript's strongest features. Instead of explicitly defining every type, the compiler analyzes assignments and expressions to infer the correct type automatically. This reduces boilerplate while maintaining type safety. However, for exported APIs and complex functions, explicit typing is generally recommended to improve readability and maintainability.
bestPractices: Use explicit types for public interfaces.
followUpQuestions: When should explicit types be preferred?

title: What are the primitive types in TypeScript?

content.overview: Primitive types represent the basic immutable data types available in TypeScript.
content.interviewAnswer: TypeScript supports all JavaScript primitive types including string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, undefined, and null. Additionally, TypeScript provides literal types that allow variables to have exact values instead of broad primitive types, enabling stronger type safety and better autocomplete.
commonMistakes: Using object instead of Object incorrectly.

title: What is the difference between any, unknown, and never?

content.overview: These three types represent different levels of type safety and compiler behavior.
content.interviewAnswer: The any type disables type checking completely and should generally be avoided because it removes TypeScript's safety guarantees. Unknown is the type-safe alternative to any. Values of type unknown must be narrowed using type guards before use, making it ideal when working with external APIs or dynamic data. Never represents values that never occur, such as functions that always throw errors or infinite loops. It is also useful for exhaustive switch statements to ensure all union members are handled.
bestPractices: Minimize usage of any in production code.
Always narrow unknown values before using them.
followUpQuestions: Why is never useful in switch statements?

title: What is the difference between interface and type in TypeScript?

content.overview: Both interface and type are used to define the shape of data in TypeScript. While they overlap in many use cases, they have different capabilities and are suited for different scenarios.
approach: Explain similarities between interface and type.
content.interviewAnswer: Interfaces are primarily designed to describe object shapes and support declaration merging, making them ideal for public APIs and library design. Type aliases are more flexible because they can represent primitives, unions, intersections, tuples, mapped types, conditional types, and function signatures. In enterprise applications, I generally use interfaces for domain models, DTOs, service contracts, and component props, while I use type aliases for complex type manipulations and reusable utility types. Choosing the right construct improves maintainability and code readability across large teams.
bestPractices: Use type for unions and advanced type manipulation.
commonMistakes: Using type everywhere without considering declaration merging.
followUpQuestions: Can a type alias extend an interface?
Which is better for React props?
