title: What are Union Types in TypeScript?

content.overview: Union types allow a variable, parameter, or return value to hold one of multiple possible types.
content.interviewAnswer: A union type represents multiple possible types using the pipe (|) operator. Instead of accepting only one type, a variable can safely store one of several predefined types. TypeScript requires developers to narrow the type before accessing type-specific members. Union types are widely used in API responses, component props, application state, and domain models where values may exist in multiple forms.
bestPractices: Use union types instead of any.
Prefer discriminated unions for complex models.
commonMistakes: Using any instead of union types.
followUpQuestions: How do unions differ from intersections?

title: What are Intersection Types?

content.overview: Intersection types combine multiple types into one using the & operator.
content.interviewAnswer: Intersection types create a new type containing all properties from multiple types. Unlike union types where a value can be one of several types, intersection types require the value to satisfy every constituent type simultaneously. They are commonly used to compose reusable models instead of creating deep inheritance hierarchies. This promotes modular design and improves maintainability in enterprise applications.
commonMistakes: Using intersections where inheritance is simpler.

title: What are Literal Types in TypeScript?

content.overview: Literal types restrict variables to exact values instead of broad primitive types.
approach: Show API and state management examples.
content.interviewAnswer: Literal types allow variables to have specific values instead of general primitive types. They improve type safety by preventing invalid assignments and enable better autocomplete. Literal types are frequently combined with union types to represent finite states such as application status, HTTP methods, user roles, or Redux action types. This approach eliminates many runtime validation errors during development.

code.snippet:
type Role = 'Admin' | 'Manager' | 'Employee';

let userRole: Role = 'Admin';

bestPractices: Replace magic strings with literal types.
commonMistakes: Using plain string instead of literal unions.
Overusing enums where literals are sufficient.

title: What are Type Assertions, and when should you use them?

content.overview: Type assertions tell the TypeScript compiler to treat a value as a specific type when the developer knows more than the compiler.
approach: Discuss angle bracket and as syntax.
content.interviewAnswer: Type assertions allow developers to override TypeScript's inferred type without changing the runtime value. They are useful when interacting with DOM APIs, third-party libraries, or dynamic data where the compiler lacks sufficient information. However, assertions should be used sparingly because they bypass type checking and can introduce runtime errors if used incorrectly. Whenever possible, prefer type guards or proper typing over assertions.

code.snippet:
const input = document.getElementById('username') as HTMLInputElement;

input.value = 'Manikandan';

commonMistakes: Using assertions to silence compiler errors.
followUpQuestions: How do type guards differ from assertions?

title: What are Type Guards in TypeScript?

content.overview: Type Guards are runtime checks that narrow a variable from a broad type (such as a union or unknown) to a more specific type, allowing TypeScript to provide accurate type checking within that code block.
approach: Explain the purpose of type narrowing.
content.interviewAnswer: Type Guards help TypeScript determine the exact type of a variable during execution. They are especially useful when working with union types, unknown values, or API responses. TypeScript supports built-in guards such as typeof, instanceof, and the in operator, as well as user-defined guards using the 'is' keyword. In enterprise applications, type guards reduce runtime errors by ensuring objects are validated before accessing their properties. I prefer using type guards instead of type assertions because they preserve type safety and make the code self-documenting.
bestPractices: Prefer type guards over type assertions.
followUpQuestions: Difference between type guards and assertions?
examples: function isString(value: unknown): value is string { return typeof value === 'string'; }
function isAdmin(user: Admin | Customer): user is Admin { return 'role' in user; }

title: Explain the typeof, instanceof, and in operators in TypeScript.

content.overview: TypeScript provides several built-in operators for runtime type narrowing, each suited for different kinds of values.
approach: Discuss when each should be used.
content.interviewAnswer: The typeof operator is used for primitive values such as string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, and undefined. The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a specific class. The in operator determines whether a property exists on an object and is commonly used for discriminating between interfaces in union types. Choosing the appropriate operator results in safer code and allows TypeScript to narrow types automatically.
commonMistakes: Using typeof on objects expecting interface checks.
followUpQuestions: How does TypeScript narrow types internally?

title: What is the difference between unknown and any? Which one should you use?

content.overview: Both unknown and any can represent values of any type, but they provide very different levels of type safety.
content.interviewAnswer: The any type disables TypeScript's type checking completely, allowing any operation without compiler errors. This defeats the purpose of using TypeScript. Unknown, on the other hand, is type-safe because it requires explicit type narrowing before the value can be used. In enterprise applications, unknown should always be preferred for API responses, external libraries, dynamic JSON, or user input because it forces developers to validate data before use.
bestPractices: Use type guards before accessing members.
followUpQuestions: How do custom type guards work with unknown?

title: What is the never type, and where is it commonly used?

content.overview: The never type represents values that never occur. It is primarily used for functions that never return and for exhaustive type checking.
content.interviewAnswer: The never type indicates that a function cannot complete normally, such as functions that always throw exceptions or run indefinitely. Another important use case is exhaustive checking of discriminated unions. By assigning the remaining value to a variable of type never, the compiler alerts developers whenever a new union member has not been handled. This makes never an excellent tool for maintaining large enterprise applications where domain models evolve over time.
bestPractices: Use never for exhaustive switch statements.
Return never from functions that always throw.

title: What is Type Narrowing, and why is it important?

content.overview: Type Narrowing is the process of reducing a broader type into a more specific type using runtime checks so that TypeScript can safely infer available properties and methods.
content.interviewAnswer: Type Narrowing enables TypeScript to determine the exact type of a variable during code execution. When working with union types, unknown values, or optional properties, the compiler initially treats variables conservatively. Through runtime checks such as typeof, instanceof, the in operator, equality checks, and custom type guards, TypeScript narrows the possible types and provides accurate IntelliSense and compile-time safety. In enterprise applications, narrowing is essential for safely handling API responses, user input, and polymorphic domain models without sacrificing type safety.

title: What are Discriminated Unions in TypeScript?

content.overview: Discriminated Unions (also called Tagged Unions) are a TypeScript pattern where multiple object types share a common literal property that allows the compiler to narrow the type automatically.
content.interviewAnswer: Discriminated Unions provide a type-safe way to model objects that can exist in multiple forms. Each object contains a common literal field, such as 'type' or 'kind', which uniquely identifies its structure. TypeScript uses this field to automatically narrow the object within conditional statements or switch cases. This pattern is heavily used in Redux actions, state machines, API response models, payment gateways, and event-driven architectures. In enterprise applications, Discriminated Unions reduce runtime errors and make future feature additions safer because the compiler ensures every case is handled.

title: What are Nullable Types, and how does strictNullChecks improve type safety?

content.overview: TypeScript treats null and undefined as distinct types when strictNullChecks is enabled, preventing accidental null reference errors.
approach: Mention optional chaining and nullish coalescing.
content.interviewAnswer: With strictNullChecks enabled, null and undefined are not assignable to every type. Developers must explicitly declare nullable values using union types such as string | null. This forces code to handle missing values safely before accessing properties or methods. Enterprise applications benefit greatly from strictNullChecks because many production bugs originate from unexpected null or undefined values. Combined with optional chaining and nullish coalescing, TypeScript significantly improves application reliability.
bestPractices: Use optional chaining instead of nested null checks.
Use nullish coalescing for default values.

title: What is the Non-Null Assertion Operator (!) in TypeScript?

content.overview: The non-null assertion operator tells the compiler that a value is definitely not null or undefined, even if its type suggests otherwise.
content.interviewAnswer: The non-null assertion operator (!) removes null and undefined from a type without performing any runtime validation. It is useful when the developer knows a value exists but the compiler cannot determine it. Common examples include DOM elements, React refs, and dependency injection frameworks. However, overusing this operator defeats TypeScript's safety guarantees. As a Team Lead, I recommend using proper type guards or optional chaining whenever possible and reserving non-null assertions for well-understood scenarios.

input.textContent = 'Hello';

Prefer optional chaining or type guards.

title: What are Optional Properties and Optional Chaining in TypeScript?

content.overview: Optional properties allow object members to be omitted, while optional chaining safely accesses nested properties without throwing runtime errors.
content.interviewAnswer: Optional properties are declared using the ? operator and indicate that a property may or may not exist. Optional chaining, introduced in modern JavaScript and supported by TypeScript, safely accesses nested properties by returning undefined if any intermediate value is null or undefined. These features simplify code, reduce nested conditional statements, and improve readability when working with partially populated API responses, configuration objects, and user preferences.

title: What is Structural Typing in TypeScript?

content.overview: TypeScript uses Structural Typing, meaning compatibility is determined by an object's shape rather than its explicit declaration or inheritance hierarchy.
content.interviewAnswer: Unlike languages such as Java or C#, which use nominal typing, TypeScript uses structural typing. Two objects are considered compatible if they have the same required properties, regardless of where they were declared. This flexibility makes TypeScript highly interoperable with JavaScript while reducing unnecessary inheritance. However, developers must be aware of excess property checks and accidental compatibility. In enterprise applications, structural typing simplifies API integration and promotes composition over inheritance, but strong domain modeling is still essential.

title: What are Generics in TypeScript, and why are they important?

content.overview: Generics allow developers to write reusable, type-safe components, functions, classes, and interfaces without sacrificing type information.
content.interviewAnswer: Generics are one of the most powerful features in TypeScript because they enable reusable code while preserving type safety. Instead of creating separate functions for different data types, we can write one generic implementation that works with any type while maintaining compile-time checking. This reduces duplication and improves maintainability. In enterprise applications, Generics are extensively used in repositories, API clients, React Hooks, Redux Toolkit, utility libraries, collections, and reusable UI components.

content.interviewAnswer: A Generic Function uses type parameters to create reusable business logic without losing compile-time type checking. Instead of writing multiple overloads for different types, one generic function can support many data types. TypeScript automatically infers the generic type in most situations, reducing verbosity while maintaining strict typing.

title: What are Generic Classes in TypeScript?

title: What are Generic Constraints in TypeScript?

content.overview: Generic Constraints restrict the types that can be passed to a generic, ensuring that required properties or methods are available.
content.interviewAnswer: Generic Constraints ensure that generic types satisfy specific requirements. By using the extends keyword, developers can require that a generic type contains certain properties or implements a particular interface. This allows reusable code while preventing invalid types from being passed. Enterprise applications frequently use constraints in repositories, sorting utilities, validation frameworks, and reusable UI components.

title: What is the keyof operator in TypeScript?

content.overview: The keyof operator produces a union of all property names of a given type. It is commonly used with Generics to build type-safe utility functions and reusable APIs.
content.interviewAnswer: The keyof operator extracts the keys of an object type as a union of string literal types. It is frequently combined with Generics to ensure only valid property names can be accessed. Instead of accepting arbitrary strings, keyof enables compile-time validation and prevents runtime errors caused by invalid property access. In enterprise applications, keyof is widely used in reusable utility functions, table components, sorting utilities, form builders, and dynamic filtering APIs.

This eliminates duplicated type definitions and keeps types synchronized with implementation. title: What are Mapped Types in TypeScript?

content.overview: Mapped Types generate new types by iterating over the properties of an existing type, making them ideal for reusable transformations.
content.interviewAnswer: Mapped Types transform existing object types by iterating over their properties. Instead of manually defining multiple versions of the same object, mapped types automatically generate new variations such as optional, readonly, nullable, or customized objects. Many built-in utility types including Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, and Record are implemented using mapped types. Enterprise applications rely heavily on mapped types for DTO transformations, API models, permissions, and reusable utility libraries.

title: What are Conditional Types in TypeScript?

content.overview: Conditional Types allow types to be selected based on compile-time conditions using the extends keyword.
content.interviewAnswer: Conditional Types enable TypeScript to choose one type or another based on whether a type satisfies a specific condition. They work similarly to JavaScript's ternary operator but operate entirely at compile time. This feature makes TypeScript extremely powerful for creating reusable libraries, utility types, API wrappers, and advanced generic frameworks. Many built-in utility types such as Exclude, Extract, NonNullable, ReturnType, and Awaited are implemented using Conditional Types.

title: What is the infer keyword in TypeScript Conditional Types?

content.overview: The infer keyword allows TypeScript to automatically infer and extract types within Conditional Types. It is commonly used to build reusable utility types such as ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited, and InstanceType.
content.interviewAnswer: The infer keyword introduces a temporary type variable inside a Conditional Type, allowing TypeScript to infer part of another type instead of explicitly specifying it. This makes advanced type manipulation possible while keeping APIs reusable. The TypeScript standard library relies heavily on infer to implement utility types like ReturnType, Parameters, ConstructorParameters, InstanceType, and Awaited. In enterprise applications, infer is useful when building reusable SDKs, API wrappers, event systems, React utility libraries, and framework-level abstractions.
bestPractices: Use infer only inside Conditional Types.

Instead of explicitly passing generic parameters, the compiler analyzes function arguments and automatically determines the appropriate types. This keeps APIs concise while preserving strong typing. title: What are the performance implications of using Generics in TypeScript?

content.overview: Generics exist only during compilation. They improve developer productivity and type safety without introducing runtime overhead.

title: Explain Partial<T> with real-world examples.

content.overview: Partial<T> makes every property in a type optional, making it useful for update operations and patch requests.
content.interviewAnswer: Partial<T> converts all properties of a type into optional properties. content.interviewAnswer: Required<T> transforms every optional property into a required property. title: Explain Omit<T, K> with real-world examples.

title: Explain Record<K, T> with enterprise examples.

content.overview: Record<K, T> creates an object type whose keys are of type K and whose values are of type T. It is commonly used for dictionaries, lookup tables, and configuration maps.
content.interviewAnswer: Record<K, T> is a utility type that creates an object where every key belongs to a specified set and every value has a consistent type. It eliminates the need to manually define index signatures and provides strong compile-time validation. Enterprise applications use Record extensively for localization dictionaries, feature flags, permission maps, configuration objects, caching, and lookup tables.
bestPractices: Avoid string index signatures when possible.
commonMistakes: Using Record when interfaces are more appropriate.
followUpQuestions: How does Record differ from index signatures?

title: Explain Exclude<T, U> with practical use cases.

content.overview: Exclude<T, U> removes types from a union that are assignable to another type. It is built using Conditional Types.
content.interviewAnswer: Exclude<T, U> creates a new union by removing all members of T that are assignable to U. It is particularly useful when restricting allowed values, filtering event types, removing deprecated states, or simplifying complex unions. Enterprise applications commonly use Exclude in permission systems, routing, feature flags, and domain models to eliminate invalid or unsupported options.
bestPractices: Prefer Utility Types over manual unions.
Keep union types small and meaningful.

title: Explain Extract<T, U> with enterprise use cases.

content.overview: Extract<T, U> creates a new union containing only the types from T that are assignable to U.
content.interviewAnswer: Extract<T, U> is the opposite of Exclude. Instead of removing matching types, it retains only the members that are assignable to another type. This utility is commonly used when narrowing event types, filtering API responses, selecting supported values, or extracting subsets of domain models. Enterprise applications use Extract in event-driven systems, routing, messaging, and complex type hierarchies.

title: Explain NonNullable<T> with real-world examples.

content.overview: NonNullable<T> removes null and undefined from a type, ensuring only valid values remain.
content.interviewAnswer: NonNullable<T> constructs a new type by excluding null and undefined from an existing type. It is especially useful after validation, data sanitization, or API response processing, where developers know a value must exist. Enterprise applications commonly use NonNullable after form validation, authentication, configuration loading, and database queries to reduce unnecessary null checks while maintaining type safety.

title: Explain ReturnType<T> with enterprise examples.

content.overview: ReturnType<T> extracts the return type of a function. It helps keep types synchronized with function implementations without duplicating type definitions.
content.interviewAnswer: ReturnType<T> is a built-in utility type that extracts the return type of a function. Instead of manually maintaining separate interfaces, developers can derive types directly from implementations, reducing duplication and improving maintainability. Enterprise applications commonly use ReturnType with service methods, Redux selectors, custom React Hooks, API wrappers, factory functions, and utility libraries to ensure that type definitions remain synchronized with implementation changes.
bestPractices: Use with factory functions and services.
Combine with typeof for reusable models.
Keep functions focused on a single responsibility.

title: Explain Parameters<T> with practical examples.

content.overview: Parameters<T> extracts a function's parameter types as a tuple, enabling reusable and type-safe APIs.
content.interviewAnswer: Parameters<T> extracts the parameter types of a function and returns them as a tuple. This utility is particularly useful when building decorators, middleware, logging systems, higher-order functions, testing frameworks, and reusable wrappers. Enterprise applications use Parameters to avoid duplicating function signatures while ensuring wrapper functions always stay synchronized with the original implementation.
bestPractices: Combine with ReturnType when building utilities.

title: Explain ConstructorParameters<T> with enterprise examples.

content.overview: ConstructorParameters<T> extracts the parameter types of a class constructor as a tuple.
content.interviewAnswer: ConstructorParameters<T> extracts the constructor parameter types from a class and returns them as a tuple. It is commonly used in dependency injection frameworks, IoC containers, testing utilities, object factories, and framework development. By deriving constructor signatures directly from classes, developers avoid duplicated type definitions and keep factories synchronized with implementation changes.

title: Explain InstanceType<T> with real-world examples.

content.overview: InstanceType<T> extracts the instance type created by a class constructor, allowing developers to reference object instances without manually defining their types.
content.interviewAnswer: InstanceType<T> derives the type of an object created by a constructor function or class. It is useful when working with dependency injection containers, object factories, plugin systems, testing frameworks, and reusable libraries. Enterprise applications benefit from InstanceType because object types remain synchronized with class implementations, reducing maintenance effort.
commonMistakes: Confusing class types with instance types.

title: Explain Awaited<T> with async programming examples.

content.overview: Awaited<T> extracts the resolved value of a Promise, making it easier to work with asynchronous code while maintaining type safety.
content.interviewAnswer: Awaited<T> unwraps the resolved type of a Promise. It supports nested Promises and accurately represents the value returned after awaiting an asynchronous operation. Enterprise applications frequently use Awaited with API services, React Query, server-side rendering, GraphQL clients, microservices, and asynchronous workflows. This utility reduces duplicate type definitions and keeps async models synchronized with service implementations.
bestPractices: Prefer async/await over nested Promise chains.
followUpQuestions: How does Awaited handle nested Promises?

title: Explain ThisParameterType<T> with practical examples.

content.overview: ThisParameterType<T> extracts the type of the explicit this parameter from a function. It is useful for building reusable utilities, decorators, middleware, and framework-level abstractions.
content.interviewAnswer: ThisParameterType<T> extracts the type of the explicit this parameter declared in a function. It enables reusable wrappers, decorators, event handlers, and middleware to preserve the correct context without redefining types manually. Enterprise applications rarely use it in day-to-day business logic but it is valuable in framework development, SDKs, plugin architectures, and libraries where preserving the execution context is essential.

Prefer arrow functions when this binding is unnecessary.

Using ThisParameterType on functions without a this parameter.

title: Explain OmitThisParameter<T> with enterprise examples.

content.overview: OmitThisParameter<T> removes the explicit this parameter from a function type, allowing it to be used as a standalone callable function.
content.interviewAnswer: OmitThisParameter<T> creates a new function type by removing the explicit this parameter from an existing function. It is useful when adapting methods into standalone callback functions or reusable utilities. Enterprise frameworks and SDKs use this utility to expose APIs without requiring callers to manually bind a context, making the APIs easier to consume.

title: What are Template Literal Types in TypeScript?

content.overview: Template Literal Types allow developers to generate new string literal types by combining existing literal types using template string syntax.
content.interviewAnswer: Template Literal Types enable TypeScript to construct new string literal types by combining existing unions. They are extremely useful for generating strongly typed event names, CSS class names, API routes, localization keys, and object property names. Enterprise applications often use Template Literal Types to eliminate invalid string values while providing excellent IntelliSense support for developers.

Combine with utility types like Capitalize.

title: What are Recursive Types in TypeScript?

content.overview: Recursive Types reference themselves to model hierarchical or nested data structures such as trees, menus, folders, and organizational charts.
content.interviewAnswer: Recursive Types are types that reference themselves, enabling TypeScript to model nested and hierarchical structures. They are commonly used for trees, menus, comments, folders, JSON objects, organizational hierarchies, and recursive configuration models. Enterprise applications rely on Recursive Types when building navigation systems, file explorers, category hierarchies, workflow engines, and nested UI components.

title: As a Team Lead, what are the best practices for using Utility Types in enterprise applications?

content.overview: Utility Types should improve maintainability, reduce duplication, and create consistent type definitions across large TypeScript codebases.
content.interviewAnswer: As a Team Lead, I encourage developers to leverage TypeScript's built-in Utility Types instead of creating duplicate interfaces. Models should have a single source of truth, with derived types created using utilities such as Partial, Pick, Omit, Readonly, ReturnType, and Awaited. Complex type transformations should remain readable, well-documented, and reviewed carefully during code reviews. Overusing advanced utility types can reduce code clarity, so it's important to balance flexibility with maintainability. Teams should establish consistent conventions for DTOs, API contracts, React props, and shared libraries to ensure long-term scalability.

title: What are Classes in TypeScript?

content.overview: Classes are blueprints for creating objects. TypeScript extends JavaScript classes by adding static typing, access modifiers, abstract classes, interfaces, and other object-oriented programming features.
content.interviewAnswer: A class is a template for creating objects that encapsulate data and behavior. TypeScript enhances JavaScript classes with static typing, access modifiers, interfaces, abstract classes, parameter properties, and readonly members. Classes improve code organization and reusability, making them suitable for modeling business entities, services, repositories, domain models, and utility libraries in enterprise applications.
bestPractices: Keep classes focused on a single responsibility.
followUpQuestions: How are classes different from interfaces?
How do classes support dependency injection?

title: Explain Access Modifiers (public, private, protected).

content.overview: Access modifiers control the visibility of class members, helping enforce encapsulation and protect internal implementation details.
content.interviewAnswer: TypeScript provides three access modifiers. 'public' members are accessible from anywhere and are the default. 'private' members can only be accessed within the declaring class. 'protected' members are accessible within the declaring class and its subclasses. Proper use of access modifiers improves encapsulation, prevents unintended modifications, and creates maintainable APIs in large applications.
bestPractices: Use protected only when inheritance is intended.

title: What are readonly properties in TypeScript?

content.overview: The readonly keyword prevents class properties from being modified after initialization, improving immutability and code safety.
content.interviewAnswer: Readonly properties can only be assigned during declaration or inside the constructor. After initialization, TypeScript prevents further modifications at compile time. Readonly is useful for identifiers, configuration values, timestamps, and immutable domain objects. Unlike const, readonly applies to object properties instead of variables.
followUpQuestions: How is immutability handled in React?

title: Explain Abstract Classes in TypeScript.

content.overview: Abstract classes provide a partially implemented base class that cannot be instantiated directly and may contain abstract members that subclasses must implement.
content.interviewAnswer: An abstract class serves as a common foundation for related classes. It can contain both implemented methods and abstract methods that derived classes must implement. Unlike interfaces, abstract classes can hold state, constructors, and shared logic. Enterprise applications commonly use abstract classes for service templates, repositories, payment processors, notification providers, and workflow engines.
bestPractices: Place shared behavior in abstract classes.
Use abstract methods for required behavior.

title: Explain Interfaces vs Abstract Classes.

content.overview: Both interfaces and abstract classes define contracts, but abstract classes can include implementation and state, while interfaces describe structure only.
content.interviewAnswer: Interfaces define contracts that classes must follow but cannot contain implementation or state. Abstract classes define a common base with shared implementation, constructors, fields, and abstract methods. Interfaces support multiple implementations, while classes can extend only one abstract class. In enterprise applications, interfaces are preferred for defining service contracts and dependency injection, whereas abstract classes are used when multiple implementations share common functionality.
bestPractices: Use abstract classes for shared logic.
commonMistakes: Replacing every interface with an abstract class.
followUpQuestions: Can a class implement multiple interfaces?
Why is multiple inheritance not supported?

title: Explain Static Members in TypeScript.

content.overview: Static members belong to the class itself rather than individual instances. They are shared across all objects created from the class.
content.interviewAnswer: Static members are associated with the class instead of its instances. They can be accessed without creating an object and are commonly used for utility methods, configuration values, constants, factory methods, counters, and singleton implementations. In enterprise applications, static members help centralize shared logic while avoiding unnecessary object creation.
bestPractices: Use static members for stateless utilities.
Avoid storing mutable global state in static properties.
Keep static methods pure whenever possible.
Use static factory methods for object creation.
commonMistakes: Using static fields as shared mutable state.

title: Explain Getters and Setters in TypeScript.

content.overview: Getters and setters provide controlled access to class properties, allowing validation, formatting, and computed values while maintaining encapsulation.
content.interviewAnswer: Getters and setters allow developers to expose properties while controlling how values are read and modified. Getters can compute values dynamically, while setters validate or transform data before assignment. Enterprise applications frequently use them for business validation, audit logging, lazy initialization, calculated fields, and enforcing domain rules without exposing internal implementation.
bestPractices: Keep getters free of side effects.
followUpQuestions: When should computed properties be used?

title: Explain Method Overriding and Polymorphism in TypeScript.

content.overview: Method overriding allows subclasses to provide their own implementation of inherited methods. This enables runtime polymorphism and flexible object-oriented design.
content.interviewAnswer: Method overriding occurs when a subclass provides its own implementation of a method defined in its parent class. This enables runtime polymorphism, allowing the same method call to behave differently depending on the object's actual type. Enterprise applications use overriding in payment gateways, notification systems, authentication providers, report generators, and workflow engines where different implementations share a common contract.

title: Explain Method Overloading in TypeScript.

content.overview: Method overloading allows multiple function signatures for the same method while sharing a single implementation.
content.interviewAnswer: TypeScript supports method overloading by allowing multiple overload signatures followed by a single implementation. The overload signatures describe the allowed call patterns, while the implementation handles all cases. Enterprise applications use overloading to build flexible APIs, SDKs, utility libraries, and service methods that support multiple input formats without sacrificing type safety.
commonMistakes: Using overloads where unions are simpler.

title: Explain Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism in TypeScript.

content.overview: Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism are three fundamental object-oriented programming principles that improve code organization, reusability, and maintainability.
content.interviewAnswer: Encapsulation hides internal implementation details and exposes only necessary functionality through well-defined APIs. Inheritance enables new classes to reuse and extend existing behavior. Polymorphism allows the same interface or method call to produce different behavior depending on the object's actual type. In enterprise applications, these principles help build scalable architectures such as payment gateways, notification systems, repositories, authentication providers, and workflow engines. However, modern applications often favor composition over inheritance to reduce coupling and improve flexibility.
bestPractices: Design against interfaces rather than concrete classes.
commonMistakes: Using inheritance when composition is more appropriate.
followUpQuestions: How does dependency injection relate to OOP?

title: What are Namespaces in TypeScript?

content.overview: Namespaces are a TypeScript feature used to organize related code under a single logical scope, helping avoid global naming conflicts. They were commonly used before ES Modules became the standard.
content.interviewAnswer: Namespaces provide a way to group related classes, interfaces, functions, and variables under a single name. Historically, they were used to organize large codebases before JavaScript supported ES Modules. Today, modern TypeScript projects use ES Modules instead of namespaces because modules provide better tooling, tree shaking, code splitting, and interoperability with modern frameworks like React, Angular, and Node.js. Namespaces are mainly encountered in legacy applications or declaration files.
bestPractices: Prefer ES Modules for modern applications.
Use namespaces only for legacy projects or declaration files.
followUpQuestions: Why are namespaces rarely used today?

title: Explain ES Modules in TypeScript.

content.overview: ES Modules are the standard module system used in modern JavaScript and TypeScript for organizing code into reusable, maintainable files.
content.interviewAnswer: ES Modules allow developers to split applications into reusable files using export and import statements. Each module has its own scope, preventing global variable conflicts. Modern frameworks such as React, Next.js, Angular, and Node.js rely on ES Modules for dependency management, tree shaking, lazy loading, and code splitting. Enterprise applications organize components, services, utilities, and business logic into separate modules to improve maintainability and scalability.
bestPractices: Prefer named exports for reusable utilities.

title: What is Declaration Merging in TypeScript?

content.overview: Declaration Merging is a TypeScript feature that combines multiple declarations with the same name into a single definition.
content.interviewAnswer: Declaration Merging allows TypeScript to merge multiple declarations with the same name into one unified declaration. This feature is commonly used with interfaces, namespaces, and module augmentation. Enterprise applications often use declaration merging when extending third-party library types, adding custom properties to Express requests, extending React component types, or augmenting SDKs without modifying their original source code.
bestPractices: Prefer module augmentation for third-party libraries.
commonMistakes: Using merging instead of proper design.

title: What are Declaration Files (.d.ts) in TypeScript?

content.overview: Declaration files describe the type information of JavaScript libraries without containing their implementation, enabling TypeScript to provide compile-time type checking.
content.interviewAnswer: Declaration files (.d.ts) provide type definitions for JavaScript code. They contain only type information and no executable implementation. TypeScript uses these files to enable IntelliSense, compile-time validation, and improved developer experience when consuming JavaScript libraries. Enterprise projects often rely on declaration files from DefinitelyTyped or create custom declarations for internal JavaScript libraries and legacy codebases.

Keep custom declaration files synchronized with implementations.

Store declaration files in a dedicated types folder.

title: Explain tsconfig.json in TypeScript.

content.overview: tsconfig.json is the configuration file that controls how the TypeScript compiler builds and validates a project.
content.interviewAnswer: The tsconfig.json file defines how TypeScript compiles a project. It specifies compiler options, source file locations, module settings, strictness rules, path aliases, output directories, source maps, and project references. In enterprise applications, tsconfig.json ensures consistent compilation across development, testing, CI/CD pipelines, and production environments while enforcing team-wide coding standards and type safety.

title: Explain important tsconfig compiler options in TypeScript.

content.interviewAnswer: Compiler options determine how TypeScript behaves during compilation. Frequently used options include target (JavaScript version), module (module system), strict (type checking), moduleResolution (dependency resolution), rootDir and outDir (project structure), baseUrl and paths (path aliases), esModuleInterop (CommonJS interoperability), sourceMap (debugging), declaration (generate .d.ts files), noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters, and skipLibCheck. title: What is Strict Mode in TypeScript?

content.overview: Strict Mode is a collection of compiler checks that enforce stronger type safety and help detect errors during development instead of at runtime.
content.interviewAnswer: Strict Mode enables a group of compiler options that make TypeScript more rigorous. It includes checks such as strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, and alwaysStrict. Enabling strict mode helps detect potential bugs early, improves IntelliSense, and increases confidence during refactoring. Enterprise projects typically keep strict mode enabled because it significantly reduces production defects.

title: Explain Source Maps in TypeScript.

content.overview: Source maps map generated JavaScript back to the original TypeScript source, making debugging easier during development.
content.interviewAnswer: When TypeScript compiles code into JavaScript, source maps create mapping information that allows browsers and debuggers to reference the original TypeScript files. This enables developers to set breakpoints, inspect variables, and view stack traces using TypeScript instead of generated JavaScript. Enterprise teams typically enable source maps during development and carefully manage or disable them in production to avoid exposing source code.

title: Explain Path Aliases and baseUrl in TypeScript.

content.overview: baseUrl and paths simplify module imports by replacing long relative paths with meaningful aliases, improving readability and maintainability.
content.interviewAnswer: Path aliases allow developers to replace long relative imports such as '../../../components/Button' with clean aliases like '@/components/Button'. The baseUrl option defines the root directory used for module resolution, while paths map alias names to physical directories. Enterprise applications rely heavily on aliases to improve readability, simplify refactoring, and organize large codebases. title: As a Team Lead, what are the TypeScript best practices for enterprise applications?

content.overview: Enterprise TypeScript development emphasizes maintainability, scalability, readability, and strong type safety rather than simply using advanced language features.
content.interviewAnswer: As a Team Lead, I encourage teams to enable strict mode, avoid the any type, and prefer unknown when dealing with uncertain data. Shared models should be reused through Utility Types rather than duplicated. Interfaces should define contracts, while abstract classes should be reserved for shared implementations. title: What are Decorators in TypeScript?

content.overview: Decorators are a special kind of declaration that can be attached to classes, methods, properties, accessors, or parameters to add metadata or modify behavior. They enable Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP)-like capabilities.
approach: Explain where decorators can be applied.
content.interviewAnswer: Decorators are functions that execute at design time and receive information about the target they decorate. They allow developers to extend or modify behavior without changing the original implementation. TypeScript supports class, method, property, accessor, and parameter decorators when experimentalDecorators is enabled. Decorators are widely used in enterprise frameworks such as Angular, NestJS, and TypeORM for dependency injection, routing, validation, authorization, logging, and metadata generation. Since the decorator proposal has evolved, developers should stay aware of differences between TypeScript's legacy decorators and the newer ECMAScript standard decorators.

title: Explain Experimental Decorators and Metadata.

content.overview: TypeScript's legacy decorators are enabled through compiler options and are commonly used with metadata reflection libraries to support dependency injection and runtime type inspection.
content.interviewAnswer: To use legacy decorators, TypeScript requires the experimentalDecorators compiler option. When emitDecoratorMetadata is enabled alongside the reflect-metadata library, TypeScript emits runtime type information that frameworks can consume. Enterprise frameworks like NestJS use metadata to automatically resolve dependencies, validate DTOs, generate API documentation, and configure routing. Developers should understand that these are legacy decorators, while ECMAScript decorators follow a newer standardized implementation.

title: What are Mixins in TypeScript?

content.overview: Mixins allow developers to compose reusable behaviors into classes without relying on deep inheritance hierarchies.
content.interviewAnswer: A mixin is a reusable class or function that adds functionality to another class. Instead of building large inheritance trees, mixins enable behavior composition. Enterprise applications use mixins for logging, auditing, permissions, timestamping, serialization, and reusable UI behaviors. Mixins align with the principle of composition over inheritance, resulting in more flexible and maintainable architectures.
bestPractices: Keep mixins focused on one responsibility.
followUpQuestions: How do React Hooks compare to mixins?

title: Explain Module Augmentation in TypeScript.

content.overview: Module augmentation allows developers to extend existing modules by adding new types, interfaces, or functionality without modifying the original source code.
content.interviewAnswer: Module augmentation enables developers to extend third-party libraries by adding additional type definitions. It is commonly used when libraries need project-specific extensions without forking or editing node_modules. Enterprise applications frequently augment Express Request objects, React types, Material UI themes, authentication contexts, and SDKs. Module augmentation works through declaration merging and helps maintain compatibility during library upgrades.
bestPractices: Store augmentations in dedicated typings files.
commonMistakes: Using augmentation instead of proper APIs.

title: What are Project References in TypeScript?

content.overview: Project References enable TypeScript projects to depend on other TypeScript projects, allowing faster builds and better scalability for large codebases.
content.interviewAnswer: Project References divide large applications into multiple independent TypeScript projects that reference one another. Each referenced project is compiled separately using the composite option, allowing incremental builds and better dependency management. Enterprise monorepos use project references to separate applications, shared UI libraries, utilities, API clients, and domain packages. This significantly improves build performance, IDE responsiveness, and maintainability for large teams.
followUpQuestions: How are project references used in monorepos?

title: Explain Incremental Compilation in TypeScript.

content.overview: Incremental compilation allows TypeScript to reuse information from previous compilations so that only changed files and their dependencies are recompiled, significantly improving build performance.
content.interviewAnswer: Incremental compilation enables TypeScript to cache project information after the initial build. During subsequent compilations, only modified files and their affected dependencies are rebuilt instead of recompiling the entire project. This dramatically reduces build times in large enterprise applications. It is commonly used with project references, monorepos, CI/CD pipelines, and IDE tooling to improve developer productivity.
bestPractices: Enable incremental compilation for medium and large projects.
Commit tsconfig.json but ignore .tsbuildinfo in version control.
Combine incremental builds with project references.
Use clean builds periodically in CI.

title: Explain Type Compatibility in TypeScript.

content.overview: Type compatibility determines whether one type can be assigned to another. TypeScript primarily uses structural typing rather than nominal typing.
content.interviewAnswer: TypeScript uses structural typing, meaning compatibility is based on the shape of objects rather than their declared names. If an object contains all required members, it is considered compatible regardless of where it was defined. This flexible approach improves interoperability between libraries and application code. Enterprise systems benefit from structural typing because DTOs, API responses, and domain models can often interact without explicit inheritance.
bestPractices: Understand structural typing before designing APIs.
Prefer explicit domain models for critical business logic.
followUpQuestions: How does compatibility affect function parameters?

title: Explain Covariance and Contravariance in TypeScript.

content.overview: Covariance and contravariance describe how subtype relationships behave in generic types and function parameters, ensuring type-safe substitutions.
content.interviewAnswer: Covariance allows a more specific type to be used where a more general type is expected. Contravariance allows a more general parameter type to replace a more specific one, primarily for function parameters. TypeScript applies these rules differently depending on compiler settings such as strictFunctionTypes. Understanding variance helps developers design safe callback APIs, event handlers, collections, and reusable generic libraries.
followUpQuestions: How does variance affect React callbacks?

title: What is Variance in TypeScript?

content.overview: Variance describes how generic types relate to one another when their type arguments have inheritance relationships.
approach: Explain covariance, contravariance, bivariance, and invariance.
content.interviewAnswer: Variance determines whether generic types preserve, reverse, ignore, or completely restrict subtype relationships. The four common forms are covariance, contravariance, bivariance, and invariance. TypeScript automatically infers variance based on how generic parameters are used. Understanding variance is especially important when designing frameworks, SDKs, reusable component libraries, event systems, and asynchronous APIs where type safety must be preserved.
bestPractices: Understand generic variance before designing APIs.

title: Explain Exhaustiveness Checking in TypeScript.

content.overview: Exhaustiveness checking ensures that every possible value in a union type is handled, preventing bugs when new union members are introduced.
content.interviewAnswer: Exhaustiveness checking is commonly used with discriminated unions to guarantee that every possible case is handled. By assigning the default branch to the never type, the compiler reports an error whenever a new union member is added but not handled. Enterprise applications use this technique in state management, reducers, workflow engines, permission systems, and API response handling to prevent runtime errors caused by missing cases.
bestPractices: Prefer switch statements for complex unions.
commonMistakes: Using string literals instead of discriminated unions.
followUpQuestions: How do reducers benefit from exhaustiveness checking?

title: What are Assertion Functions in TypeScript?

content.overview: Assertion functions allow developers to tell the TypeScript compiler that a condition is guaranteed to be true after the function executes. They improve type safety while validating data at runtime.
content.interviewAnswer: Assertion functions use the 'asserts' keyword to narrow types after runtime validation. Unlike type guards that return a boolean, assertion functions throw an error when validation fails and inform the compiler that execution can continue only if the condition is satisfied. Enterprise applications use assertion functions to validate API responses, configuration values, authentication contexts, environment variables, and user input before executing business logic.

Use assertion functions for critical validations.
Keep assertions focused on one responsibility.
commonMistakes: Replacing all type guards with assertions.

title: Explain Branded Types (Nominal Typing) in TypeScript.

content.overview: Branded types simulate nominal typing in TypeScript by attaching unique markers to primitive types, preventing accidental assignment between logically different values.
content.interviewAnswer: TypeScript is structurally typed, meaning compatible shapes are interchangeable. Branded types introduce unique compile-time markers to distinguish values that share the same primitive type but represent different concepts. This prevents bugs such as assigning a ProductId where a UserId is expected. Enterprise systems commonly use branded types for identifiers, account numbers, currencies, order numbers, and security-sensitive values.
bestPractices: Use branded types for domain identifiers.
Keep branding internal to the domain layer.

Exposing branding details throughout the application.

title: What is the satisfies Operator in TypeScript?

content.overview: The satisfies operator verifies that an expression conforms to a type while preserving the expression's most specific inferred type.
content.interviewAnswer: Introduced in TypeScript 4.9, the satisfies operator validates that an object conforms to a required type without changing its inferred literal types. Unlike type assertions, satisfies performs compile-time validation while preserving precise inference. This makes it ideal for configuration objects, route definitions, theme configurations, localization files, feature flags, and API metadata in enterprise applications.
bestPractices: Use it instead of unsafe type assertions.
Combine with literal types for stronger inference.
commonMistakes: Using satisfies where type assertions are required.

title: Explain Const Assertions (`as const`) in TypeScript.

content.overview: Const assertions tell TypeScript to infer the narrowest possible types for literals while making object properties and array elements readonly.
content.interviewAnswer: Using 'as const' prevents TypeScript from widening literal values. Object properties become readonly, array literals become readonly tuples, and string or number literals retain their exact values. Enterprise projects commonly use const assertions for Redux action types, route definitions, feature flags, configuration objects, permission maps, and API endpoint declarations where immutable literal values are required.
bestPractices: Use as const for immutable configuration.
Leverage const assertions with literal unions.

title: Explain Type Predicates (`value is Type`) in TypeScript.

content.overview: Type predicates allow developers to create custom type guard functions that help the compiler narrow types during control flow analysis.
content.interviewAnswer: A type predicate is a function whose return type uses the syntax 'value is Type'. When such a function returns true, TypeScript narrows the variable to the specified type. Type predicates are widely used when processing API responses, validating user input, handling polymorphic data, parsing JSON, and implementing reusable validation libraries. They improve readability while maintaining strong compile-time type safety.
bestPractices: Keep type guards small and reusable.
commonMistakes: Using type assertions instead of predicates.

title: Explain Type-safe API Design in TypeScript.

content.overview: Type-safe API design ensures that requests, responses, errors, and domain models are validated at compile time, reducing runtime failures and improving developer productivity.
content.interviewAnswer: Type-safe APIs use strongly typed request and response models, Generic interfaces, discriminated unions for error handling, and shared contracts between frontend and backend. Enterprise applications often generate TypeScript types from OpenAPI or GraphQL schemas to eliminate duplication and ensure consistency. Generic API clients, DTOs, validation libraries, and strict compiler settings further improve reliability. A well-designed type-safe API reduces runtime errors, improves IDE support, simplifies refactoring, and enables safer collaboration across teams.

Validate runtime data using schema validation libraries.

title: What are TypeScript Performance Optimization Techniques?

content.overview: Large TypeScript projects can experience slower compilation and IDE responsiveness. Optimizing compiler configuration and project architecture significantly improves developer productivity.
content.interviewAnswer: Performance optimization involves enabling incremental compilation, using project references, organizing applications into smaller modules, avoiding excessively complex Generic types, reducing unnecessary type computations, and limiting deep recursive conditional types. Enterprise teams also leverage path aliases, separate development and production configurations, distributed CI builds, and caching provided by tools such as Turborepo or Nx. Profiling compiler performance helps identify bottlenecks before they impact developer productivity.

content.interviewAnswer: Enterprise monorepos organize applications, shared UI libraries, utilities, API clients, and domain packages into separate TypeScript projects. Project references, path aliases, incremental compilation, and composite builds improve scalability and reduce build times. Tools such as Nx, Turborepo, Rush, and pnpm workspaces coordinate builds, dependency graphs, testing, and caching. title: What is Node.js?

content.overview: Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime built on Google's V8 JavaScript engine. It allows developers to execute JavaScript outside the browser and is optimized for building fast, scalable, event-driven server-side applications.
approach: Discuss architecture and common use cases.
Highlight why it is popular for backend development.
content.interviewAnswer: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime environment built on the V8 engine. Unlike browsers, Node.js provides APIs for interacting with the operating system, file system, networking, and processes. It uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model that makes it highly efficient for handling thousands of concurrent connections. Node.js is commonly used for REST APIs, GraphQL servers, real-time applications, microservices, streaming platforms, and serverless functions.
bestPractices: Keep Node.js updated for security patches.
commonMistakes: Assuming Node.js is multithreaded for JavaScript execution.
followUpQuestions: When should Node.js not be used?

title: How does Node.js work internally?

content.overview: Node.js combines the V8 JavaScript engine, the libuv library, the event loop, and asynchronous system APIs to efficiently execute JavaScript and handle I/O operations.
content.interviewAnswer: When Node.js starts, V8 compiles JavaScript into machine code. JavaScript executes on a single thread, while libuv handles asynchronous operations such as file access, networking, timers, and DNS using the operating system and its thread pool. Once asynchronous work completes, callbacks are queued and executed by the event loop. This architecture enables Node.js to efficiently serve many concurrent requests without creating a thread per request.
commonMistakes: Thinking asynchronous code runs on the JavaScript thread.
Using CPU-intensive tasks on the event loop.
followUpQuestions: How does the event loop work?

title: What is the Event Loop in Node.js?

content.overview: The Event Loop is the core mechanism that allows Node.js to perform non-blocking asynchronous operations while executing JavaScript on a single thread.
content.interviewAnswer: The Event Loop continuously checks for completed asynchronous operations and executes their callbacks when the JavaScript call stack becomes empty. It processes work through several phases including timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check, and close callbacks. Combined with libuv, the event loop enables Node.js to handle thousands of concurrent operations without creating one thread per request.
commonMistakes: Blocking the event loop with heavy computation.

title: Explain the Node.js Architecture.

content.overview: Node.js follows an event-driven, non-blocking architecture built on the V8 engine and libuv, enabling scalable I/O-intensive applications.
content.interviewAnswer: Node.js architecture consists of the V8 JavaScript engine, the event loop, libuv, asynchronous operating system APIs, and a thread pool for certain I/O operations. Incoming requests are handled by the event loop without allocating a separate thread for each client. Long-running I/O operations are delegated to libuv or the operating system, allowing Node.js to serve thousands of concurrent clients efficiently while using minimal resources.
commonMistakes: Running expensive loops on the main thread.

title: Single Thread vs Multi Thread in Node.js.

content.overview: Node.js executes JavaScript on a single thread while leveraging libuv's thread pool and the operating system to perform asynchronous operations concurrently.
content.interviewAnswer: Node.js is often described as single-threaded because JavaScript executes on one main thread. However, asynchronous I/O operations are delegated to libuv and the operating system, which use background threads where appropriate. For CPU-intensive workloads, Node.js provides Worker Threads to execute JavaScript in parallel, while the Cluster module allows multiple Node.js processes to utilize multiple CPU cores. Enterprise applications typically combine asynchronous I/O, worker threads, clustering, load balancers, and containers to achieve high scalability.

code.snippet:
const { Worker } = require('worker_threads');

new Worker('./worker.js');

bestPractices: Use Worker Threads for CPU-intensive tasks.
Use Cluster or process managers for multicore CPUs.
commonMistakes: Believing Node.js cannot use multiple cores.
Executing CPU-intensive work on the event loop.

title: What is Non-blocking I/O in Node.js?

content.overview: Non-blocking I/O allows Node.js to initiate input/output operations without waiting for them to complete. Instead, the application continues executing other code while libuv and the operating system handle the I/O in the background.
approach: Explain how libuv handles asynchronous operations.
content.interviewAnswer: Non-blocking I/O is one of Node.js's core strengths. When an I/O operation such as reading a file, querying a database, or making a network request is initiated, Node.js delegates the task to libuv or the operating system instead of waiting. The JavaScript thread remains free to process other requests. Once the operation completes, its callback or Promise is placed into the event loop queue. This enables Node.js to efficiently handle thousands of concurrent connections using minimal threads.
bestPractices: Prefer asynchronous APIs over synchronous ones.
Use Promises or async/await for better readability.
Stream large files instead of loading them entirely into memory.
commonMistakes: Using synchronous APIs in web servers.
Assuming asynchronous operations execute on the JavaScript thread.
Blocking the event loop with CPU-intensive work.
followUpQuestions: How does libuv implement non-blocking I/O?
What operations use the thread pool?
When should synchronous APIs be used?

title: Blocking vs Non-blocking Code in Node.js.

content.overview: Blocking code prevents the JavaScript thread from executing other tasks until the current operation completes, while non-blocking code allows execution to continue immediately.
content.interviewAnswer: Blocking operations stop the execution of the JavaScript thread until they finish. Examples include synchronous file reads or CPU-intensive loops. Non-blocking operations return immediately, allowing Node.js to continue processing other requests while asynchronous work executes in the background. For production applications, asynchronous APIs should be preferred because they maximize concurrency and improve response times.
bestPractices: Move CPU-intensive tasks to Worker Threads.
commonMistakes: Running expensive loops on the main thread.
followUpQuestions: Can blocking operations ever be acceptable?

title: What are Streams in Node.js?

content.overview: Streams are objects that allow data to be processed incrementally rather than loading everything into memory at once, making applications more memory-efficient and scalable.
content.interviewAnswer: Streams process data in small chunks as it becomes available. Instead of loading an entire file into memory, Node.js reads or writes data incrementally. Streams are ideal for handling large files, media streaming, HTTP responses, log processing, and real-time data pipelines. Because they consume less memory and start processing immediately, streams significantly improve application performance.
commonMistakes: Loading large files entirely into memory.

title: What are the Different Types of Streams in Node.js?

content.overview: Node.js provides four types of streams: Readable, Writable, Duplex, and Transform. Each serves a specific purpose for handling data flow.
content.interviewAnswer: Readable streams allow data to be read, Writable streams allow data to be written, Duplex streams support both reading and writing, and Transform streams modify data while passing it through. These stream types form the foundation of Node.js file processing, networking, compression, encryption, and HTTP communication.
bestPractices: Implement Transform streams for data processing.

title: What are Buffers in Node.js?

content.overview: Buffers are objects used to store raw binary data. They enable Node.js to efficiently process data received from files, network sockets, streams, and binary protocols.
content.interviewAnswer: Buffers are fixed-size memory allocations used to store binary data outside the V8 heap. Since JavaScript strings are UTF-16 encoded, Buffers provide an efficient mechanism for working with binary formats such as images, videos, PDFs, TCP packets, and encrypted data. Buffers are widely used with streams, file systems, HTTP communication, and cryptographic operations.
bestPractices: Use Buffer.from() instead of deprecated constructors.
Use streams for very large binary data.
commonMistakes: Loading massive files into Buffers unnecessarily.
followUpQuestions: How are Buffers used with streams?

title: What is EventEmitter in Node.js?

content.overview: EventEmitter is a core Node.js class that enables event-driven programming by allowing objects to emit named events and register listeners to respond when those events occur.
content.interviewAnswer: EventEmitter is part of Node.js's events module and forms the foundation of its event-driven architecture. It allows objects to emit events using emit() and register listeners using methods like on() and once(). Many built-in Node.js modules, including streams, HTTP servers, file system watchers, and process events, are implemented using EventEmitter. This pattern promotes loose coupling between components and enables asynchronous communication.
bestPractices: Remove unused listeners to prevent memory leaks.

title: How does require() work in Node.js?

content.overview: The require() function loads CommonJS modules, executes them once, caches the result, and returns the exported object for reuse throughout the application.
content.interviewAnswer: When require() is called, Node.js resolves the module path, loads the module if it hasn't already been loaded, executes the module code, caches the exported object, and returns it. Future require() calls return the cached version instead of executing the module again. This caching mechanism improves application performance and ensures singleton behavior for shared modules.
bestPractices: Keep modules focused on a single responsibility.
commonMistakes: Expecting modules to execute on every require().
followUpQuestions: How does require() resolve module paths?

title: CommonJS vs ES Modules in Node.js.

content.overview: CommonJS and ES Modules are two module systems supported by Node.js. CommonJS uses require() and module.exports, while ES Modules use import and export statements.
content.interviewAnswer: CommonJS is the original module system in Node.js and loads modules synchronously using require(). ES Modules (ESM) are the standardized JavaScript module system using import and export. ESM supports static analysis, tree shaking, top-level await, and better compatibility across browsers and Node.js. Modern enterprise projects generally prefer ES Modules for new applications, while CommonJS remains common in legacy codebases and existing npm packages.
bestPractices: Use ES Modules for new projects.

title: What is package.json?

content.overview: package.json is the central configuration file for a Node.js project. It contains project metadata, dependencies, scripts, version information, and package configuration.
content.interviewAnswer: The package.json file defines the identity and configuration of a Node.js application. It includes the project name, version, description, dependencies, development dependencies, scripts, engines, and module type. npm and other package managers use this file to install packages, execute scripts, and manage application metadata. Every production Node.js project should include a well-maintained package.json.

title: package-lock.json vs yarn.lock.

content.overview: package-lock.json and yarn.lock lock dependency versions to ensure consistent installations across different environments and team members.
approach: Compare npm and Yarn lock files.
content.interviewAnswer: package-lock.json is generated by npm, while yarn.lock is generated by Yarn. Both files record the exact versions of installed dependencies and their transitive dependencies. This guarantees that every developer, CI pipeline, and production deployment installs identical package versions, reducing 'works on my machine' issues. A project should use only one package manager and commit its corresponding lock file to version control.

title: What is npm?

content.overview: npm (Node Package Manager) is the default package manager for Node.js. It helps developers install, update, remove, and manage third-party libraries and project dependencies.
content.interviewAnswer: npm is the official package manager bundled with Node.js. It provides access to the world's largest package registry, allowing developers to reuse open-source libraries instead of writing everything from scratch. npm manages project dependencies, executes scripts defined in package.json, publishes packages, and resolves dependency trees. Enterprise projects rely on npm for dependency management, version control, CI/CD integration, and package publishing.

title: Difference between npm, npx, and Yarn.

content.overview: npm, npx, and Yarn are tools for managing JavaScript packages. npm installs packages, npx executes packages without permanently installing them, and Yarn is an alternative package manager focused on performance and dependency management.
content.interviewAnswer: npm is the default package manager used to install and manage dependencies. npx is bundled with npm and allows developers to execute packages directly without installing them globally. Yarn is an alternative package manager that offers faster installations through caching, deterministic dependency resolution, and workspace support. Today, npm has adopted many Yarn features, so both are commonly used in enterprise applications.

title: What is libuv in Node.js?

content.overview: libuv is a cross-platform C library that provides Node.js with its event loop, asynchronous I/O, thread pool, networking, and operating system abstractions.
content.interviewAnswer: libuv is the backbone of Node.js's asynchronous architecture. It manages the event loop, asynchronous file system operations, timers, networking, DNS lookups, and a thread pool used for operations that cannot be handled asynchronously by the operating system. JavaScript itself runs on a single thread, while libuv coordinates background work and notifies the event loop when operations complete. This architecture allows Node.js to efficiently handle thousands of concurrent requests.

title: How does the V8 Engine work in Node.js?

content.overview: V8 is Google's high-performance JavaScript engine that compiles JavaScript directly into optimized machine code instead of interpreting it line by line.
content.interviewAnswer: The V8 engine parses JavaScript source code into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), generates bytecode using the Ignition interpreter, and then optimizes frequently executed code using the TurboFan Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler. V8 also includes an efficient garbage collector for automatic memory management. In Node.js, V8 is responsible for executing JavaScript, while libuv handles asynchronous I/O and the event loop.

Use the latest Node.js LTS version.

title: How does Node.js execute JavaScript?

content.overview: Node.js executes JavaScript using the V8 engine while coordinating asynchronous operations through libuv and the Event Loop.
approach: Explain interaction between V8 and libuv.
content.interviewAnswer: When a Node.js application starts, V8 parses the JavaScript source code, converts it into bytecode, and compiles frequently executed sections into optimized machine code. Synchronous JavaScript runs on the main thread. Whenever asynchronous APIs such as file system operations, networking, or timers are encountered, Node.js delegates them to libuv or the operating system. After these operations complete, callbacks are placed into the Event Loop queues and executed once the call stack becomes empty. This separation between JavaScript execution (V8) and asynchronous processing (libuv) enables Node.js to efficiently handle many concurrent requests.
bestPractices: Move CPU-intensive work to Worker Threads.

title: What is the fs module in Node.js?

content.overview: The fs (File System) module provides APIs to interact with the file system. It supports reading, writing, updating, deleting files and directories using both synchronous and asynchronous methods.
approach: Explain the purpose of the fs module.
content.interviewAnswer: The fs module is one of Node.js's core modules used for interacting with the file system. It provides methods for creating, reading, updating, deleting, renaming, copying, and watching files and directories. Most production applications use the asynchronous Promise-based or callback-based APIs because they don't block the Event Loop. Enterprise applications commonly use the fs module for log management, configuration loading, file uploads, report generation, and temporary file handling.

title: What is the path module in Node.js?

content.overview: The path module provides utilities for working with file and directory paths in a platform-independent manner.
approach: Explain why the path module exists.
content.interviewAnswer: The path module simplifies working with file system paths across different operating systems. Instead of manually concatenating strings, developers can safely build, normalize, resolve, and parse file paths. It automatically handles path separators for Windows and Unix-based systems, making applications portable across environments.
bestPractices: Use path.join() instead of string concatenation.

title: What is the os module in Node.js?

content.overview: The os module provides operating system-related information such as CPU details, memory usage, platform, hostname, network interfaces, and user information.
content.interviewAnswer: The os module exposes information about the underlying operating system. Developers can retrieve CPU information, total and free memory, operating system type, platform, hostname, architecture, uptime, temporary directories, and network interfaces. Enterprise applications use this module for diagnostics, health monitoring, deployment validation, and infrastructure reporting.

title: What is the process object in Node.js?

content.overview: The global process object provides information and control over the currently running Node.js process.
content.interviewAnswer: The process object is globally available in every Node.js application. It provides access to command-line arguments, environment variables, process ID, memory usage, uptime, current working directory, signals, and lifecycle events. Enterprise applications commonly use process.env for configuration, process.exit() for graceful shutdowns, and process.on() to handle termination signals and uncaught exceptions.

title: What is the child_process module in Node.js?

content.overview: The child_process module enables Node.js applications to create and communicate with additional operating system processes.
approach: Explain why child processes are needed.
content.interviewAnswer: The child_process module allows Node.js to spawn new operating system processes for executing external programs or scripts. It provides methods such as spawn(), exec(), execFile(), and fork(). Unlike Worker Threads, child processes have separate memory spaces and communicate using IPC (Inter-Process Communication). They are commonly used for executing shell commands, image processing, video transcoding, build automation, and running isolated services.
bestPractices: Validate user input before executing commands.

title: What is the Cluster module in Node.js?

content.overview: The Cluster module allows a Node.js application to create multiple worker processes that share the same server port, enabling applications to utilize all available CPU cores.
content.interviewAnswer: By default, Node.js executes JavaScript on a single thread, utilizing only one CPU core. The Cluster module solves this limitation by spawning multiple worker processes, each running its own event loop and V8 instance. The primary (master) process distributes incoming connections among workers, allowing the application to scale across all CPU cores. Since workers are isolated processes, a crash in one worker usually doesn't affect the others. Modern production environments often use PM2, Docker, Kubernetes, or cloud load balancers instead of directly managing the Cluster module.

Monitor worker crashes and restart automatically.
Use PM2 or Kubernetes in production.
commonMistakes: Using Cluster for CPU-intensive tasks instead of Worker Threads.
